Katalog Berita (Halaman 27/57)

#6107. Delta CEO: “Customers Are Not Choosing Airlines Based On Wi-Fi”

I’ve gotta be honest, I don’t envy the situation that Delta CEO Ed Bastian is in. Unlike most other carriers in the United States, Delta hasn’t opted for SpaceX Starlink Wi-Fi, and has instead gone with Amazon Leo.

In theory that’s fine, except Amazon Leo is years behind Starlink, and just faced a new setback, due to a rocket failure. Elon Musk has also repeatedly publicly ridiculed Bastian, regarding what Bastian reportedly said about Musk to employees.

There’s now an interesting update, as Bastian made some comments about the carrier’s Wi-Fi choice, and overall customer preferences. It sure is amazing how narratives can change, based on what’s convenient…

This week at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum 2026, Delta’s CEO was asked about the carrier’s decision not to choose Starlink, plus the public spat with Musk. Here’s what Bastian had to say about this:

“We’ve been the leader in Wi-Fi, and in free and fast Wi-Fi, and we’ve been at it for five years. I’ve got a long history with Elon on that. We’ve looked at Starlink, we actually helped them started in aviation, we gave them our planes to use during COVID, when we weren’t flying, and they tested the system out. We just couldn’t come to agreement on a business model.”

“We’ve been the leader in free, fast Wi-Fi. We are confident there will be more than one LEO product in the world other than Starlink, and I’m confident Amazon has the capability to do a great job. Customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi. We’ve been out with a great product from Viasat, which we’ve got two new satellites in the sky. It’s not Starlink caliber but it’s pretty darn close.”

“This is about the total experience, and customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.”At the #F500Innovation Forum, @Delta CEO Ed Bastian told @ajs that the airline helped Elon Musk’s satellite Wi-Fi “get started in aviation,” but the two sides “just couldn’t come to… pic.twitter.com/xmSERJNjjH

Look, before I get too deep into this, let me make several points that I think no one reasonable will disagree with (which is not to say some commenters won’t disagree!):

When Bastian formally unveiled plans for free Wi-Fi at CES 2023 in Las Vegas, he said the following:

“At work, at home and everywhere in between, connectivity is essential to daily life, and your journey on Delta should be no different. Our vision has long been to deliver an experience at 30,000 feet that feels similar to what our customers have available on the ground.”

“We didn’t just want free Wi-Fi to offer base-level service – we wanted it to be transformative for the entire onboard experience. It is imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home, and we’ve put this system through meticulous tests to make that possible.”

Earlier this year, when announcing plans to partner with Amazon Leo for connectivity, Bastian said that “we need to stay the leader” in inflight connectivity. Obviously that won’t be the case for a long time.

As I see it, Delta’s problem here is pretty simple. Customers absolutely notice a difference between Viasat and Starlink. The issue isn’t that people will stop flying Delta altogether. The issue is that Delta has built its entire brand on being the industry leader, and on being on the forefront of technology.

There’s no denying that this sentiment among the public changes over time, because inflight Wi-Fi is easily one of the top amenities that passengers notice nowadays. Seriously, I can’t count the number of people I’ve heard from or just overheard talking about their first Starlink experience, and how blown away they were.

I guess to look at it from another angle, there’s no airline that loves talking about how premium it is more than Delta. What makes Delta premium? If we’re going to believe that Delta is premium, it’s not based on any one single thing, but rather, it’s based on the sum of the experience. And I think anyone who thinks a major Wi-Fi disadvantage lasting for years isn’t part of what contributes to consumer sentiment is lying to themselves.

Delta CEO Ed Bastian is now downplaying the importance of inflight Wi-Fi. He’s arguing that “customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi,” which in isolation, is probably true. But he’s also arguing that Viasat is “pretty darn close” to Starlink, which is most definitely not true, as I see it.

I wouldn’t be so critical of these statements if it weren’t for Bastian spending years hyping up how it’s “imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home,” while also saying “we need to stay the leader.” And for that matter, Delta has of course also long hyped how premium it is — if that’s to be believed, it’s not about any one feature, but instead, it’s about the sum of the experience.

What do you make of Bastian’s inflight connectivity comments?

Holding one United card generally doesn't prevent you from opening another or earning its welcome bonus. Chase allows you to apply for multiple United cards, as long as they are separate cards.

For example, if you already hold an , you can also apply for a . However, you can't hold two of the same card, so if you have a Quest card, you can't get a second in order to double up on its benefits.

There's one exception: If you are an existing United Club Visa Signature cardmember (no longer available to new applicants), you are not eligible for the current United Club card.

Yes, you can have multiple United credit cards at one time. Unlike some other airline credit cards, United's cards don't have a broad restriction that prevents you from holding multiple cobranded cards.

Holding multiple United cards won't make sense for infrequent flyers, since benefits like free checked bags and priority boarding overlap on multiple cards. Yes, you can get the same United credit card more than once. However, you will only earn another welcome offer if you no longer hold that card and at least 24 months have passed since you received the new-cardmember bonus.

If you are an authorized user on someone else's United card, Chase does not consider that being a current cardholder for the purposes of that card's bonus restrictions. In other words, you can still apply for your own version of that card and earn its welcome bonus.

#6104. An Airline You’ve Never Heard Of Will Fly From Seoul Incheon To Los Angeles

A very small international airline plans to add long haul, international flights to the United States as of next spring, and I feel pretty confident in saying that 99% of people have never heard of this airline (I had to look it up after seeing one of their planes at an airport several weeks back, and I know a thing or two about identifying airplanes). 😉

As reported by AeroRoutes, as of May 1, 2027, Parata Air will launch daily nonstop flights between Seoul Incheon (ICN) and Los Angeles (LAX). The flight will operate with the following schedule:

WE301 Incheon to Los Angeles departing 12:00PM arriving 7:20AMWE302 Los Angeles to Incheon departing 9:50AM arriving 3:20PM (+1 days)

Parata Air will operate the route with an Airbus A330-200, featuring 260 seats, including 18 business class seats and 242 economy seats. The 5,944-mile flight is blocked at 11hr40min eastbound and 13hr30min westbound.

Tickets on the flight are now on sale, and I see fares starting at around $670 one-way in economy, and around $2,500 one-way in business class. Those aren’t exactly terribly attractive fares for a newcomer that appears to have a pretty lackluster onboard product.

For those not familiar with Parata Air, the airline launched operations back in 2019, but it has a fleet of just a handful of planes, including three Airbus A330s and two Airbus A320s. This will be the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. As I hinted at in the headline, I imagine this is a fully unknown player to most people, and I had never heard of the airline until a few weeks ago.

Random thought — can anyone think of a smaller international airline (in terms of fleet size) that added long haul flights to the United States? I know that’s very specific, but I can’t think of another one… it’s possible I’m missing something, though!

The airline acquired its three A330s secondhand from different sources, with the planes having flown for Garuda Indonesia, Hainan Airlines, and Thomas Cook (though that plane doesn’t have business class).

The Seoul Incheon to Los Angeles market is pretty well served in terms of capacity, but not so well served in terms of competition. That’s because no US carrier flies between Los Angeles and Seoul Incheon, and with Korean Air having acquired Asiana, there’s now only one South Korean flag carrier.

If you look at the market, you’ll see that Korean Air operates up to four daily flights, and Air Premia operates up to two daily flights. Now we’ll see a third airline from the country operating in the market, though with the lowest capacity, and arguably the worst product.

It’ll be interesting to see when we see some competition here on the US side. Delta might operate the route eventually, but that doesn’t actually increase competition, since the airline has a joint venture with Korean Air. American has (smartly, probably) given up on Los Angeles as a long haul hub. So that leaves United, and I could definitely see the airline eventually adding service in the market, as a competitive response against Delta and Korean Air, if nothing else.

As of May 2027, Parata Air will be launching a new nonstop route between Seoul Incheon and Los Angeles, representing the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. The airline will be operating daily in the market with Airbus A330s. With this, there will be three South Korean carriers flying this route, though no airlines from the United States.

What do you make of this new Parata Air service?

#6103. Delta SkyMiles Blue Amex Review: Is The No Annual Fee Card Worth It?

American Express and Delta have had a close relationship for many years, and as part of that, they issue seven co-branded Delta Amex cards. This is my in-depth Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card review, as this is the entry-level personal Delta credit card with no annual fee (Rates & Fees), and probably the least talked about card in the lineup. It’s far from the most rewarding Delta credit card, but if you want to earn Delta miles and only fly the airline occasionally, it could be worth a look.

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card

Before I get into the full Delta Blue Amex Card review, here’s an overview of the card’s main features, from its welcome bonus and earning rates, to other benefits:

Beyond that, here are my thoughts on the pros and cons of the Delta Blue Amex:

When applying for a credit card, the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and fees, are obviously major factors that people consider. With that in mind, let’s take a look at those details for the Delta Blue Amex Card. As you’d expect for this card, the lack of fees largely comes at expense of a smaller welcome offer.

The Blue Delta SkyMiles Amex has a welcome offer of 10,000 bonus SkyMiles after spending $1,000 within the first six months of your card membership. Based on my latest points & miles valuations, Delta SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each, making this bonus worth $110. We’ve seen this card’s bonus go a bit higher, but not by a huge amount.

The bonuses on all other Delta Amex cards are significantly higher, which isn’t a surprise, since cards with annual fees often have better bonuses than cards without annual fees. It’s hard to get excited about that offer, but I guess something is better than nothing?

The welcome offer on the Delta Blue Amex Card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available to you if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past. The rules go beyond that, though.

You’re actually not eligible for the bonus on the card if you have or have had any of the more premium versions of the Delta Amex card portfolio, at least among the personal cards. This is true across the portfolio, and the idea is that you’re always eligible for the bonus on a more premium card, but not eligible for the bonus on a less premium card.

So if you do want to pick up multiple Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to first apply for the Delta Blue Amex, then the Delta Gold Amex, then the Delta Platinum Amex, and then the Delta Reserve Amex (or at least you’ll want to move in that general order).

Beyond that, Amex’s general card application restrictions apply, including that you can typically have at most five credit cards from Amex at a time (that doesn’t include hybrid cards).

Let me emphasize once again that the Blue Delta Amex has no annual fee. It’s great to see a trend whereby we’re seeing more airline credit cards with no annual fees, since it’s a nice option for someone who wants a co-branded credit card, but doesn’t want to pay an annual fee.

You can also add additional users to the card at no extra cost.

There’s no doubt that card issuers are moving toward offering more no annual fee cards with no foreign transaction fees, though it’s still not the standard. The Blue Delta Amex has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), which is awesome, since most Amex no annual fee cards do still have these fees.

When it comes to earning rewards, the Blue Delta SkyMiles Credit Card offers:

For a no annual fee product, it’s nice to see a card offering a bonus on dining. While some bonus categories are better than none, I don’t find the bonuses to be particularly compelling, as there are still better cards out there for airfare purchases and restaurant purchases.

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or on Delta’s SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

The Delta Blue Amex is a decent no annual fee card in the sense that it offers 2x miles at restaurants and has no foreign transaction fees, but how are the perks on the card? Not surprisingly, this is an area where the card lags, and where the cards with annual fees offer significantly more value.

Nonetheless, there are some perks to the card that may prove valuable to the occasional Delta flyer.

If you have the Blue Delta Amex, then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food or alcoholic beverages, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

Having the Blue Delta Amex makes you eligible for the Delta Pay With Miles program. What is that? This allows those with co-branded Delta Amex cards to redeem miles for one cent each towards a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles towards flights, and then they still earn elite miles for taking those flights.

In other words, the 10,000 miles available as part of the welcome offer can be redeemed for a minimum of $100 worth of travel on Delta. This is obviously the lowest cost option for unlocking that benefit.

The Delta Blue Amex includes access to dedicated entrance lanes and fast lanes at stadiums and arenas that participate in the Amex Venue Collection program. As part of this benefit, you can also get 10% back on qualifying concessions purchases, up to $250 back per calendar year. (Enrollment required)

Amex Offers is a program that offers discounts for purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

The ideal situation is to have a no annual fee card (like this one), so you can get access to these offers without paying an annual fee to get access to this.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page.

The Delta Blue Amex comes with some basic travel and purchase protection benefits:

There are some coverage limits and exclusions to be aware of, so you’ll want to review the full details in the card’s benefits guide before assuming you’re insured.

Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

Many people who like Delta as a brand may be tempted to pick up the Delta Blue Amex — it allows you to earn miles with Delta, it has no annual fee, and it offers some perks that could add value (20% off inflight purchases, Amex Offers, access to Delta Pay With Miles, etc.).

However, in general, I wouldn’t recommend outright applying for this card:

Let me address both of those points below.

If you’re considering the Delta SkyMiles Blue Amex, let me make the case for applying for the Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (learn more) instead, which currently has the limited-time offer:

You can always get the Gold Delta Amex, and then if you don’t find it to be worth the annual fee, you can downgrade it to the Blue Delta Amex after a year. That would allow you to maintain the card account, and you wouldn’t pay the annual fee when you downgrade (and you’d still get the elevated perks and bigger bonus for the first year).

At a minimum, it really is worth trying the Delta Gold Amex to see if you like it and to take advantage of the better bonus, and then you can downgrade at a later point if you find it’s not worthwhile.

If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. That’s because these points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers 4x points at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year and then 1x) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 in purchases per calendar year and then 1x), and 3x points on flights booked directly with airlines or at AmexTravel.com. That’s a much better return than you’ll get on this card, and it’s also quite easy to make the math on the card work.

If you’re absolutely committed to having a no annual fee card and want to maximize your return on spending, there are lots of excellent no annual fee cards to consider.

My favorite is the Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more). The card earns 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase (in the form of ThankYou points).

But it gets even better than that — rewards earned on this card can be converted into ThankYou points at a 1:1 ratio and can be moved to partner programs at the best possible ratio, assuming you have the card in conjunction with one earning premium ThankYou points, like the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more).

That means the card earns two ThankYou points per dollar, and I value those points at 1.7 cents each, so that’s like a 3.4% return on everyday spending.

I appreciate that American Express and Delta offer a no annual fee option with the Delta Blue Amex. For someone absolutely committed to getting a Delta Amex Card and not paying an annual fee, this is the best/only option.

The card has no foreign transaction fees, offers 2x miles on dining, and gives you access to Pay With Miles and 20% discounts on inflight purchases.

However, for most people, I think it’s worth applying for the Delta Gold Amex. The card has a lot more perks and a much better bonus, and you can always downgrade the card to the Delta Blue Amex after at least a year.

Squeezing the most value out of every dollar on a cruise is a top goal for most travelers. It doesn't matter if you're on a quick escape cruise from a local port or an exotic luxury cruise halfway around the globe, you never want to end it feeling like you should have gotten more for your money.

Cruises are the ultimate all-inclusive vacation, with meals, transportation and entertainment included, and there is even more value-adds on board that you may have never thought to look for. The trick is to hone in on built-in value early, in the cruise shopping and purchasing stage, and then pay attention to every detail that might enhance your experience along the way. Here are 14 tricks to get the most possible value from any cruise you take.

It can feel like you’re bombarded with emails after you book a cruise, but some of them contain hidden treasure.

Royal Caribbean, Celebrity, Princess, MSC and Virgin Voyages are among the cruise lines that use a bidding process to manage unsold cabins as the sailing date gets closer. Carnival Cruise Line offers upgrades without bidding. Pay attention to your email, and you might nab a nicer cabin for less than you’d pay by booking it outright.

Emails also alert you to discounted packages or bundles for Wi-Fi, shore excursions, specialty dining, drinks and even spa treatments. Much of the same information can be found on the cruise planner on the cruise line's website, but unless you log in often, watch those emails for value-oriented offers.

While it's tempting to always look at the newest (and often the biggest) ships, you may find that switching to an older or smaller ship, which may be just slightly less in demand, often helps squeeze more from your cruise budget without limiting your vacation fun.

You can also save hundreds of dollars by opting for inside staterooms, rooms with partially blocked views or those with less-than-perfect locations on the ship. This even works within suite zones or exclusive ship-within-a-ship areas. My dermatologist recently confided that he always chooses an inside suite within the Yacht Club when he cruises with MSC; he gets all the VIP perks, including exclusive dining and entertainment venues, for thousands less than the suites with balconies.

And don't rule out the cruise cabin guarantee option. Regardless of the cabin type, allowing the cruise line to select your stateroom is almost always the better value option than picking a specific room.

While most lines sign you up for loyalty programs automatically after your first sailing, you might need to opt in. Some lines allow you to sign up even before your first cruise, giving you advance offers to entice you to go ahead and book that first cruise.

Status matches between cruise lines are a huge bonus. MSC offers a status match with other cruise lines, hotel brands and tour operators. You can do this before your first booking and get Voyagers Club benefits on your first cruise with the line. These could be as simple as a welcome beverage or as elaborate as a complimentary tasting menu dinner. Ultra-luxury sister brand, Explora Journeys, offers a one-time status match with MSC and comparable luxury lines.

Royal Caribbean, Celebrity and Silversea have an ongoing status match across the three sister brands. That means you can reap rewards on a luxury line by earning status on a mainstream brand.

Similarly, Viking’s loyalty program spans its river, ocean and expedition arms. Once you’ve cruised with the line, you’ll get benefits fleetwide, even if you try out a different kind of ship.

Some lines offer casino status matches with land- and sea-based casinos that might even earn you a free cruise. These often come with exceptions; your casino status on Carnival won't get you a free cruise on sister line Princess, but casino status on Celebrity might. And don't be afraid of free cruise certificates handed out by reputable casinos on land where you have status. They’re the real deal, often based on long-standing partnerships between the casino and cruise lines. The reverse is also true. I’ve never been to WinStar Casino in Oklahoma, but they send me offers of free hotel nights using postcards featuring the Carnival logo, with which I have casino status.

While not every loyalty perk holds a huge value for you, little freebies definitely add up on vacation. For example, Carnival gives you a free 1.5-liter bottle of water on your second cruise. That's one less bottle you might have to buy.

As you move up the loyalty ladder, cruise by cruise, the perks improve. For example, you may be eligible for free laundry, drinks and specialty dining the higher up you go. I once met a couple who were on a five-night Royal Caribbean cruise for the sole purpose of moving up to the top loyalty tier before going on a much longer cruise. The higher tier would give them free Wi-Fi and a handful of other valuable perks for the duration of their longer cruise.

Often the onboard perks are loaded on your cabin keycard, but you might have to ask how to use them. For example, if you are entitled to a free bag of laundry at your loyalty level, nobody will hand you a bag and say, "Fill it up; it's free." It's up to you to know the perks you are entitled to and follow through on getting them.

Amid the barrage of marketing messages for beverage packages of all sorts, it's easy to forget that certain beverages are included in your cruise fare.

Every cruise ship offers standard drip coffee, water, iced tea, hot cocoa, punch or lemonade and a variety of tea bags free of charge. Milk and juice are available at breakfast. Look for self-serve stations at the buffet, or ask your server.

Sodas are included on premium lines like Windstar, Oceania and Viking, as well as on luxury lines like Seabourn, Silversea and Regent Seven Seas Cruises. Disney Cruise Line also offers free soft drinks but only from the beverage dispensers by the pool.

It's surprising how many free (or included) alcoholic drinks you can procure once on board a ship. I've been offered sparkling wine at art auctions, galley tours and captain's events.

Royal Caribbean and Celebrity both have free drinks for the top three tiers of loyalty status.

Celebrity Cruises offers free drinks for anyone gambling in the casino. Carnival and Virgin Voyages are among the lines offering free drinks to select gamblers based on their prior gambling history. You might be eligible for those, even if you only gamble on land.

The cabin you book might come with valuable perks, so know what they are so you don’t miss out.

For example, Celebrity’s AquaClass cabins come with not only thermal suite access and exclusive dining in the line’s health-forward restaurant called Blu, but also a choice of exercise equipment. Yoga mats are supposed to be in the closet when you board, but you'll have to ask for any of the other items listed on the menu provided.

Suites on most lines come with extra perks like included drink packages and specialty dining. On certain ships, even some smaller suite categories come with exclusive dining rooms only for the occupants of those categories. The food in these exclusive eateries is often a step above the main dining room and not to be missed if you are staying in the entitled category.

The same goes for suite lounge access. You generally find snack and beverage stations stocked with specialty treats you won’t find elsewhere on board, making it worthwhile to at least sneak a peek at the lounge offerings if you paid for a category that comes with access.

The cost of going out to the movies these days makes a cruise movie night a big value. Now that most of us watch movies by streaming them at home, actually going to the movies is a treat in and of itself.

Movie nights on a ship are a step above your local movie theater. You might enjoy films on a giant poolside screen while you float in the pool or relax on a lounge chair with bar servers bringing the drinks to you. Disney Cruise Line screens first-run films for free, with costumed characters in attendance. Many lines serve free popcorn wherever movies are being shown.

If staying in for a movie night in your jammies sounds good, take advantage of free or pay-per-view movies on your cabin’s TV. Disney is among the cruise lines with popcorn on the room service menu. On a Silversea cruise, I once told our butler we were staying in for an evening movie. His immediate reply was, "Shall I pop some corn for you?" The answer, of course, was, "Yes, please."

Live music, comedy acts, magic shows and musical theater are luxuries you can pay dearly for on land — but all of those are available on cruise lines at no charge. The larger the ship, the more entertainment options you will have.

Free live music is found daily in lounges, pool areas, atriums and on stage in the main auditorium. Audience participation game shows, sometimes raucous in nature, usually take over lounge space a few nights of the cruise.

The main stage will have a show nightly, either song-and-dance revues featuring an onboard cast or guest magicians, musicians and comedians, some with TV credits to their name. Larger ships might have separate comedy club venues to keep the laughs flowing every night of the cruise, with both family-friendly and adults-only shows. Clubs on dry land where these same performers appear often charge a $30-40 cover. On a recent Carnival cruise, I estimate my visits to the comedy club alone would have cost me several hundred dollars.

Some lines lean heavily into specialty performances. Look for ice skating, aquatic high-diving and dance shows on select Royal Caribbean ships and acrobatic performances on Virgin Voyages and MSC Cruises. Royal Caribbean and Norwegian Cruise Line both offer Broadway musicals, while Disney produces live musical performances based on its popular animated movies.

With so much free entertainment that would certainly cost a family hundreds in ticket prices on land, you’ll get a ton of value from your cruise if you attend the shows that most appeal to you.

When the night's entertainment winds down, it's time to dance the night away and go clubbing — and cruise ship clubs don’t have a cover. Big ships crank up the party vibe after the last show in the main theater, so you can make the most of every second you’re awake. Hop from dance parties on the pool deck to karaoke in smaller bar venues and even silent discos in the atrium to keep the fun going into the wee hours.

Eating out and trying local restaurants are hallmarks of vacation, but you can blow your budget doing that on land. You can spend a lot on specialty restaurants on board, too, but pay attention to timing to get the most value out of the free dining on board. If you know you would enjoy steak and lobster, do a little research to figure out which night they will be served in the main dining room. You don’t want to find out too late that you booked a specialty restaurant on the same night you could have been eating surf and turf at no additional cost. Themed brunches and afternoon tea are also main dining room events you don’t want to miss.

Looking beyond the buffet and main dining room might turn up surprising food choices you didn't even know were included in your cruise fare. Pool grills serving juicy hamburgers, specialty coffee shops with snacks and even sandwiches and healthy choice salads near the solarium are all yummy examples of freebies tucked away in spots you might not think to look.

As for the specialty restaurants, those are generally still a bargain compared to a similar meal at a land-based restaurant. Carnival's Steakhouse is a good example. The cost is $52 per person. That sounds steep, but if you've priced a filet mignon in a nice restaurant lately, you'll know that $52 barely covers the steak. At Fahrenheit 555, you'll be treated to appetizers, sides and desserts, making the cover charge a vacation value. Book your Steakhouse dinner for the first night of a sailing, and Carnival will usually throw in a complimentary bottle of house wine.

For lounging in your cabin, free or low-cost room service boosts your cruise value. My personal favorite (especially on sea days) is enjoying a "first breakfast" of coffee and croissants from room service before heading out for a more substantial second breakfast.

Private island experiences provide an inexpensive break from paying for excursions in other ports. First things first, the beach is free. Use of the lounge chairs is free (not always the case at some vacation destinations). Swimming in the ocean and in some pools is free.

Depending on the island, you might find hammocks, hiking trails, game and sports areas and interesting snorkeling spots. Rental equipment for snorkeling and other water activities is usually reasonably priced, but you can bring your own gear.

The major private islands all have complimentary barbecue buffets and occasionally other food trucks or fast-casual offerings. As with specialty dining on the ship, even the up-charged food won’t cost as much as at a theme park or on the beach at a vacation destination.

Relying on shore excursions offered by the cruise line is the easy way to plan your days in port. It also keeps you safe from becoming one of those pier-running late-comers at departure time. Those tours are not always the best value, however. Lower-priced reputable port tours may take a bit more research on your part, but can save hundreds of dollars.

I recently enjoyed a 4-hour kayak tour in Ketchikan with pickup near the pier and guaranteed on-time return that I booked directly on the Ketchikan Kayak Company's website, which saved me roughly $60 per person compared to the similar tour offered by the ship.

And don’t forget that skipping organized tours altogether can also net you an amazing day in port. If tours aren't your jam, or you just don’t want the scheduling hassle in every port, consider simply venturing out on your own in search of fun. If the town is walkable, start with that. Or consider renting a car or simply hiring a taxi driver. I've visited Cozumel dozens of times on cruise ships, but had never seen the far side of the island. Last fall, a group of friends and family rented two Jeeps online from a rental agency located walking distance from the pier. We had a marvelous time stopping wherever we wanted, including for an impromptu tequila tasting (for the non-drivers, of course).

Whether you're talking about something as simple as miniature golf, basketball, pickleball or table tennis, or as elaborate as surf simulators and multideck dry slides, cruise lines often load their ships’ upper decks with free fun. As with all things on a cruise, certain activities come with a cost, but you’ll find plenty of fun that does not add to your cruise bill.

On land, you typically need to pay to access waterslides, splash parks, rock climbing walls and adventure and zip lines, but on many cruises, these active onboard attractions come free. Certain activities might require reservations or specific attire (like closed-toe shoes), so check out the details in advance.

Did you know that some cruise lines let you buy VIP packages pre-cruise for a bundle of preferential treatment similar to suite category perks? The real value of these programs lies in not paying for an expensive suite while enjoying extra perks as if you did.

Royal Caribbean's The Key includes early boarding times, a welcome lunch, fast lane access to select onboard activities, premium theater seating, departure day perks and free internet access for each guest who purchases the package.

Celebrity's Premium Access is a similar bundle. The combination of complimentary room service and Premium Wi-Fi for two devices makes this package a cruise value.

Holland America's Club Orange includes a complimentary cabin upgrade when available, priority check-in, priority lines at Guest Services and Shore Excursion desks, bathrobes, an expanded room service menu, a complimentary glass of sparkling wine, exclusive events like behind-the-scenes tours and coffee chats with performers and even separate dining rooms on some ships. With a bit of strategy, the cabin upgrade alone can justify the cost of the Club Orange add-on. This works best in Oceanview and Verandah categories where you can choose an obstructed view cabin at a low cost, banking on the Club Orange upgrade to a full-view room.

Carnival’s Faster to the Fun offers early cabin access, express luggage delivery and priority check-in and embarkation, shuttle boarding, dining reservations, Guest Services line and debarkation. Note that Carnival blocks access to FTTF for some loyalty guests, including some casino loyalty members, to avoid stacking of perks.

Norwegian Cruise Line’s Priority Access includes priority security, check-in and boarding processes on embarkation day, plus skip-the-line tendering and debarkation, complimentary standard room service and a $50 spa discount on port days.

Cruises come with so much value bundled into the cost of the fare that it can be easy to overlook all the goodies that aren't costing you anything extra. Adding value to your cruise vacation can be as simple as reading the daily planner or taking a walk around the ship to discover all the included attractions. Whether it’s free entertainment in your favorite lounge, a dance lesson or no-cost prime rib in the main dining room, all those onboard freebies and low-cost add-ons make it possible to get outsize value from your cruise vacation.

#6101. Surprise: Aer Lingus Unveils First-Ever Premium Economy, Coming To 10 A330s

Aer Lingus is getting on the premium economy hype. The Irish flag carrier has today announced it will introduce the cabin for the first time on 10 of its Airbus A330s, which will also feature new business and economy cabins (the product won’t be coming to the Airbus A321LR/XLR fleet).

This is quite a big change, and one that should give it a leg up in the highly competitive trans-Atlantic market.

The cabin will feature just four rows with 28 seats in a 2-3-2 configuration. That’s about average when compared to other premium economy cabins. The narrow fuselage of the A330 means there’s only room for three seats in the middle section, rather than the four many other airlines offer.

As for the soft product, Aer Lingus promises three-course dining, drinks throughout the flight, a pillow and blanket, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing (not noise-canceling) headphones.

I actually really like the design and color scheme. It’s modern, looks elegant and premium, and most importantly of all for the airline of the Emerald Isle, the colors are quintessentially Irish.

Aer Lingus says premium economy fares will start from 700 Euros one-way, putting a return trip at around 1,400 Euros. That works out to around $1,534, and a few hundred dollars cheaper than United’s nonstop fares from Newark (EWR) to Dublin (DUB).

We’ll have to wait until October 1 next year to try Aer Lingus’ new premium economy out for ourselves. The airline hasn’t yet announced which routes will get the product first, but we should find out in the coming months.

The good news is, they’ll operate on many of the airline’s 18 nonstop routes from Dublin to the United States.

As a small, almost boutique-style airline with just 63 aircraft, Aer Lingus must remain competitive, especially in the saturated transatlantic market in which it predominantly operates. The addition of premium economy bridges the large gap between economy and business, and should open the airline up to a potential new customer base who’ve never flown it before.

I’ll be attending an event in Dublin tonight, so I should be back with more images and extra info soon!

What do you make of Aer Lingus’ new premium economy?

#6100. Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Sources said Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”

The post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He said the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

In 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

After Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

“The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker said. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this important position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Collins said in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

#6099. You Can Transfer British Airways Avios To Someone Else For $11 Using The Finnair Loophole

British Airways charges most members £50 per transaction to give Avios to someone else, and each transfer tops out at 60,000 points. Move the same points through Finnair and you can give someone 100,000 Avios for a single €10 fee. You can move British Airways Avios into a Finnair account, and Finnair charges €10 to transfer Avios to another member. I’ve written about moving Avios between airline programs to get the best redemption deal. The same flexibility lets you choose which program’s rules to use when giving points to another person. For two people with British Airways balances, the process is: Each person links their own British Airways and Finnair accounts. Names and email addresses need to match within each person’s accounts, and both programs need two-factor authentication enabled. The person giving the points moves their Avios into their own Finnair account. That transfer is free and 1:1. They use Finnair Shop’s transfer function to send the Avios to the other person’s Finnair account, paying €10. The recipient can use the points through Finnair or move them into their own linked British Airways account, again free at 1:1. Under the British Airways transfer terms, sending 100,000 Avios takes two transactions at £50 apiece, or the equivalent charged in your home currency (Gold members are exempt from that fee). Senders and recipients are each limited to 200,000 Avios per calendar year. Finnair doesn’t cap the amount or frequency of member transfers beyond your available balance. However, moving the points between airlines has its own limits. Open the accounts in advance. Finnair requires an account to be at least 30 days old to link with another Avios program. The sender must have been a member for at least 90 days to transfer to another person online. Finnair allows newer members to transfer via customer care at a higher €20 transfer fee. This route is for adults. Linking requires members to be at least 18, and you can’t transfer Avios into a Finnair Plus Junior account. Transfer ceiling. Finnair allows 1–999,999 Avios per cross-program transaction. Basic members have a shared 1 million Avios limit over 12 months, counting all linked programs and both directions. Higher tiers don’t have that 12-month cap. You may not need to pay anything. British Airways’ free household account pools balances for redemptions, and you can often simply book an award for someone else. But this lets you do it without restricting redemptions from your account to members of your household account. Don’t leave the points sitting in a dormant Finnair account. Transfers don’t restart their 18-month expiration clock. One Reddit member reported losing newly transferred Avios less than two weeks later because the Finnair account was already inactive. You can move British Airways Avios into a Finnair account, and Finnair charges €10 to transfer Avios to another member.

I’ve written about moving Avios between airline programs to get the best redemption deal. The same flexibility lets you choose which program’s rules to use when giving points to another person.

For two people with British Airways balances, the process is:

Under the British Airways transfer terms, sending 100,000 Avios takes two transactions at £50 apiece, or the equivalent charged in your home currency (Gold members are exempt from that fee). Senders and recipients are each limited to 200,000 Avios per calendar year.

Finnair doesn’t cap the amount or frequency of member transfers beyond your available balance. However, moving the points between airlines has its own limits.

You may not need to pay anything. British Airways’ free household account pools balances for redemptions, and you can often simply book an award for someone else. But this lets you do it without restricting redemptions from your account to members of your household account.

Don’t leave the points sitting in a dormant Finnair account. Transfers don’t restart their 18-month expiration clock. One Reddit member reported losing newly transferred Avios less than two weeks later because the Finnair account was already inactive. They subsequently reported getting the points back after contacting the airline.

There shouldn’t need to be loopholes for this. Transferring points you already own should be free. We ought to properly regulate these corporate pseudocurrencies to include basic consumer protections—like free transfers, advance notice for program changes, and stabilized values—so these stealth devaluations stop. You’d think the banks underwriting these multi-billion-dollar currencies would want stability, too, before constant devaluations burn out the consumers fueling their credit card portfolios.

Wasn’t there an old Court case involving UA and a customer over the “meaning” of lifetime membership in their Club? If memory serves, the court sided with airline saying lifetime is what the airline says. What you describes a similar case.

The 30-day account age rule is the part I’d flag for anyone trying this in a hurry — you really do need to set the Finnair accounts up well ahead of time. The expiry warning matters too: moving points doesn’t restart that 18-month clock, so it’s worth checking the receiving account is active before sending a large balance across. For smaller gifts, the household account route Gary mentions is probably simpler, but for a one-off larger transfer this €10 path is hard to beat.

@alanZ — H’yup. Lagen v. United Continental Holdings. Flyer spent years working towards United’s million-miler program, which promised ‘premier executive’ status. But, when United merged with Continental, and slashed those perks, he sued for breach of contract. 7th Circuit sided with airline, citing MileagePlus rules, which gave United the unilateral right to modify, devalue, or terminate program benefits “on a whim” with or without notice. I prefer Judge Hamilton’s dissent, which notes an airline’s definition of ‘lifetime’ means: “Lifetime, unless we change our mind.” So, like I’ve been saying, we can close this regulatory vacuum, if we wanted, but we haven’t in the US at least for now.

#6098. Barry Goldwater Saw a Way Out of the Wilderness

No matter how federal elections turn out, there’s always work to be done at the state and local levels.

Senator Barry Goldwater addresses supporters in Arizona during his 1964 presidential campaign.

Hulton-Deutsch Collection/Corbis via Getty Images

Barry Goldwater was acquainted with political setbacks. The morning after the 1964 presidential election, he could count the states he had won on two hands. Harder to number were the Americans who had spent that fall knocking on doors for the first time because a senator from Arizona had given voice to something they believed. Goldwater had asked them to help Americans reclaim power from Washington.

After the loss, Goldwater urged his supporters not to give up the fight for free markets, smaller government, and the American family. It was the collective conviction that Americans could build better lives for their families if they could keep more of what they earned and decide for themselves how to raise their children that kept these people invested in American politics.

Victor Riches is the President and CEO of the Goldwater Institute, leading the Institute’s efforts to help people in all 50 states live freer, happier lives.

#6097. Aer Lingus Retrofitting A330s With New Business, Premium Economy, Economy Cabins

It’s not just Aer Lingus’ premium economy stealing the headlines in Ireland today. Expected to fly passengers for the first time on October 1, 2027, the new cabins are part of a comprehensive Airbus A330 tip-to-tail retrofit that will include new business and economy cabins. We covered the premium economy cabin in a separate article story.

The same 10 Airbus A330s that will get the airline’s new premium economy will also get a swanky new business class. The airline’s Airbus A321XLRs aren’t included in this cabin update.

Aer Lingus opted for its take on the ever-popular Collins Elevation suite. There’ll be 28 seats in a 1-2-1 configuration that stretch out to 78 inches long when in lie-flat mode.

The color palette of Irish greens, whites, and light wood gives the seat an elegant yet distinctly non-corporate feel. It’s a thumbs-up from me.

In terms of updated tech, each seat has 4K HD screens (in all cabins) as well as wireless and USB-C charging. While nothing revolutionary, these touches will significantly modernize Aer Lingus A330 cabins.

Aer Lingus is also introducing a self-service bar stocked with snacks and drinks. I wonder if this will include Champagne…

The airline will also serve up a whole new in-flight dining experience featuring dishes inspired by both Irish ingredients and its transatlantic destinations.

It wouldn’t be a full retrofit without sprucing up economy.

Per the renderings, Aer Lingus has done a great job again with the cabin’s look and feel. The emerald green Shamrocks are a lovely touch.

Seats are configured in the A330’s classic 2-4-2 configuration — a favorite for those traveling in pairs.

While the recline looks a bit modest here, the seat’s thickness looks like it’ll provide more support than some of those ultra-thin, rigid seats airlines are sneaking in these days.

The six-way adjustable headrests should also mean less head-wobbling when catching some shut-eye.

The curved design of the seat backs should hopefully mean noticeably more knee space.

Aer Lingus is also upping its food and beverage ante for economy passengers. In addition to a snack bar, a new mid-flight snack will be offered.

A retrofit program like this was essential for Aer Lingus to remain competitive in the transatlantic market. The introduction of premium economy was a great move, especially since the cabin is known to be highly profitable.

Aer Lingus has also done a great job of matching the Irish color scheme and sleek design across all cabins, which is more than can be said for some airlines these days. 😉

What do you make of Aer Lingus’ new A330 cabins?

#6096. New Hyatt Credit Card Offer: Earn 4 Free Nights—Why I Spend On The Card Towards Elite Status

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The World Of Hyatt Credit Card (See rates and fees) has a new initial bonus: earn 4 free nights at any Category 1-4 Hyatt hotel or resort after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. That’s an improved offer from a card whose bonuses have usually been more modest than competing travel cards.

I have this card, and I put actual spending on it. Hyatt points are still valuable, but what gets me to use the card is the credit toward elite status and the rewards earned along the way. Hyatt status does more to improve my hotel stays than status with other major chains.

These are four separate certificates, so you can use them for one trip or spread them across different stays. You’ll need standard room award availability, and the certificates expire 12 months after they’re issued. The terms require checkout before the expiration date. Under Hyatt’s current award chart, a Category 4 standard room can cost as much as 25,000 points per night. Four certificates could therefore cover nights that would otherwise require 100,000 points. Their category restrictions and expiration date make them less flexible than having those points in your account. The card has a $95 annual fee. Chase excludes current holders of this card and previous cardmembers who received its initial bonus within the past 24 months. The usual Chase restriction on applicants who’ve opened five or more personal cards in the past 24 months also generally applies. Why I Keep The Card And Spend On It The annual Category 1-4 free night after each cardmember anniversary makes the $95 fee easy to justify. There’s also a second Category 1-4 night after $15,000 in purchases during a calendar year which makes that spending more rewarding. And these nights are transferable to another World of Hyatt member. If I won’t use one, I can give it to someone who will. For spending, the card earns 4 Hyatt points per dollar on qualifying Hyatt purchases; 2 on restaurants, airline tickets bought directly from airlines, local transit and commuting, and fitness club and gym memberships; and 1 on other purchases. More significantly, it comes with 5 qualifying nights each year, plus 2 more qualifying nights for every $5,000 spent. Those nights count toward both status and Milestone Rewards. Put $15,000 of otherwise unbonused spending on the card during a calendar year and you earn: 15,000 Hyatt points. An additional Category 1-4 free night certificate. 6 qualifying nights from spending, giving you 11 including the card’s annual 5. That means 49 qualifying nights actually spent in hotels, plus the card’s 5 annual nights and 6 from spending, gets you to the 60 needed for Globalist. And the $5,000 spent earning the initial bonus counts toward the $15,000 free-night threshold in the calendar year when you spend it. Milestone Rewards start at 20 qualifying nights and continue every 10 nights through 150. Some of the rewards on the way to Globalist are: Qualifying Nights Notable Rewards 30 A Category 1-4 free night, plus a choice of additional reward. 40 A Guest of Honor Award, plus a choice that includes a Suite Upgrade Award. 50 A choice that includes 2 Suite Upgrade Awards. 60 Globalist status, a Category 1-7 free night, 2 Suite Upgrade Awards, 2 Guest of Honor Awards, and My Hyatt Concierge. The value of another $5,000 in spending depends on where those two nights get me. Crossing a threshold for suite upgrades or Globalist can be worth giving up a higher earning rate on another card. Hyatt Status Is Stronger Than At Other Major Chains The card itself comes with Discoverist status. That’s better than a hole in the head as my grandfather used to say. But reaching Globalist has real value – as well as the milestone choices along the way. The biggest benefit is confirming a suite at the time of booking with a Suite Upgrade Award for up to seven nights when an eligible standard suite is available for the stay. That’s a huge value on family trips. I also value having a My Hyatt Concierge I can email requests to, actual delivery of 4 p.m. late checkout at eligible properties, and a more generous breakfast benefit than I get from other chains. At participating hotels without an available club lounge, Globalist breakfast generally covers a full breakfast for up to two adults and two children registered in the room, including tax and gratuity. Late checkout has exceptions, including availability limits at resorts, but I’m usually proactively offered late checkout everywhere else (and personally find it honored more often than not at resorts). The Free Night Certificates Should Be More Flexible The current version of this card launched in 2018. Its annual certificate is still capped at Category 4, while category creep has taken away many of the hotels where I’d most want to use it. Just this year, 14 hotels moved from Category 4 to Category 5, including Hyatt Regency Seattle, Hyatt Regency Grand Cypress and Hyatt Regency Jersey City. Five moved the other way, bringing options like Hyatt Centric Congress Avenue Austin and Dream Nashville within reach, but the certificate lost more hotels than it gained. I’d like Hyatt to at least let members add points to a certificate to book a higher category. The certificate works at a Category 4 hotel charging 25,000 points, but won’t work at a Category 5 hotel when it’s charging 15,000 points. And I wish Hyatt would let us combine these free nights with Suite Upgrade Awards or Guest of Honor Awards. I value them most traveling with my family when I’m paying for rooms out of pocket. That’s always when I want to use my suite upgrades! I don’t need a suite on a business stay (paid by someone else, when it’s just me) or to use the free night award. FWIW a free tool like HotelPriceTracker emails you when a rate drops, so you get a feel for what a night really costs over a few weeks. IMO if you’d use 2 of the 4 the card pays for itself, if not skip it

I think the category creep is happening across the hotel credit cards. Bonvoy now allows you to top up the points on their “free night” from the included 80,000 all the way up to 100K. Coincidentally, check out how many hotels seem to require 103K points for redemption.

I think Hyatt could also benefit from a more premium card. I’d pay the $800 fee for a higher level card like Hilton and Marriott offer. Have it include a Category 7 or 8 night, get me Explorist, and a path to Globalist. I’d sign up or upgrade in a minute

@1990 — Oops, just saw your question – I did! learned a lot about Marriott brands seeing that I never stay there without a bank program incentive, heh

#6095. Chase Ink Business Preferred Card Bonus: 100K Points Welcome Offer

The Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card has a phenomenal sign-up bonus of 100,000 points after spending $8,000 within three first three months, and there’s lots of value to this card in the long term, especially thanks to its reasonable $95 annual fee — read my Ink Preferred review here. If you’re eligible for the card, there’s no reason not to apply.

This is part of the Chase Ink Business card portfolio, and it’s arguably Chase’s most rewarding and best value business credit card. In this post I’d like to go over the Ink Business Preferred bonus details, including eligibility requirements.

Link: Learn more about the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card with 100K bonus points

The Chase Ink Preferred Card currently has a welcome offer of 100,000 Ultimate Rewards points after spending $8,000 within the first three months.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Chase Ultimate Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each, meaning the 100,000 points are worth $1,700 to me, which is among the best bonuses out there. There are lots of great uses of Chase points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners.

Chase Ultimate Rewards partners with programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, British Airways Club, United MileagePlus, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, World of Hyatt, and more. If you want to cash out Chase points (which I wouldn’t recommend), you can get one cent of value per point, meaning the 100,000 points would be worth $1,000.

Just to give some examples of possible uses of the points, you could transfer 34,000 points to Iberia Club for a one-way Iberia business class ticket from Boston to Madrid, or 60,000 points to Flying Blue for a one-way Air France or KLM business class ticket from Miami to Paris. You can stretch your points even further by taking advantage of transfer bonuses.

Let me emphasize that the Chase Ink Preferred 100K bonus is the best publicly available sign-up bonus that’s currently available on the card, and it has been the standard offer since November 2025. How do the previous Chase Ink Preferred offers compare, though?

As you can see, the Ink Business Preferred sign-up bonus on the card has varied from 80,000 points to 120,000 points, and the current bonus of 100,000 points is 10,000 points better than the previous offer, which was for up to 90,000 points.

Everyone has to decide for themselves if it’s worth waiting for the possibility of another welcome bonus of over 100,000 points. Personally I probably wouldn’t wait, since we have no reason to believe such an offer is returning soon. Furthermore, with the card’s useful points categories for spending, there’s potentially quite an opportunity cost to waiting. But still, if you’re in no rush, it could be worth waiting.

When it comes to getting approved for the Chase Ink Preferred Card and earning the welcome bonus, what rules should you be aware of? Well, there are the card specific policies, and then also the more generic Chase policies. When you pull up the application, you’ll see the following terms:

The new cardmember bonus may not be available to you if you have ever had this card. We may also consider factors pertinent to your business in determining your bonus eligibility.

As you can see, officially the welcome bonus may not be available to you if you currently have this card, or if you’ve had it in the past. However, eligibility for the card (including the bonus) is unrelated to whether you have any other Chase business card.

In other words, you’re eligible for this card, including the bonus, if you have other cards from Chase, including cards in the business lineup. Speaking of which, those cards have some amazing bonuses as well, which are worth considering:

Beyond that, there are some general Chase rules to be aware of:

While Chase business cards can be tough to get approved for, they offer such fantastic bonuses and perks, so it’s worth the effort, in my opinion. Furthermore, it’s nice how the eligibility requirements aren’t too strict in terms of qualifying for the bonus.

The Chase Ink Preferred Card has a $95 annual fee (with no cost for additional employee cards), and offers all kinds of amazing perks that make it worth holding onto. Among other things, here’s what makes the card so valuable:

Let me acknowledge that the Ink Preferred isn’t right for everyone. As I see it, the Ink Preferred is all about the rewards structure and the strong purchase and travel protection, while also having a reasonable cost. If you’re looking for airport lounge access or a card with all kinds of premium perks and credits, then consider the Sapphire Reserve Business, which many people will find to be worthwhile for the Chase Sapphire Lounge access, Priority Pass membership, travel credits, and more.

The Chase Ink Preferred Card is one of the best business cards out there, and if you’re eligible for the card, there’s lots of merit to applying.

Not only does the card have a big bonus, but it’s worth holding onto for the great rewards structure, excellent protection benefits, and the ability to maximize other cards in the Chase ecosystem. With the changes we’ve seen to other Chase cards in recent times, this card is arguably even more compelling than in the past.

Do you have the Chase Ink Preferred Card, and if so, what has your experience been?

#6094. Democrats Have the Electoral College in Their Sights

Will the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact soon cross the 270-vote threshold?

Delegates point to an electoral map at the Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia, Pa., in 2016.

The blue wave washed over a slew of state legislative chambers and six new governorships. Next year, a majority of Americans will live in a state with a Democratic governing trifecta. One of the biggest dangers of Democrats’ new political clout is that they will now push to override the Electoral College and effectively force the country into a nationwide presidential popular voting system as early as 2028.

Their vehicle is called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their electoral votes to the winner of the national popular vote, no matter which candidate carries each state. The compact was born after former President George W. Bush’s narrow Electoral College victory in 2000, and it was turbocharged following Donald Trump’s 2016 win despite his losing the popular vote. The District of Columbia and 18 states have joined, accounting for 222 electoral votes.

John Fund is National Review’s national-affairs reporter.

#6093. Trump’s ‘invasion’ asylum ban to face justices

The border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

“The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition says.

Trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”

Last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

The case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

#6092. 3 Women Stranded By FAA Nationwide Ground Stop Bought A $48,000 Ford Bronco—Then Drove 27 Hours Home

Three women stranded in Charlotte after Friday’s nationwide flight grounding bought a $48,000 Ford Bronco and drove 27 hours home to North Dakota. They’d gone away for work training. They came home with a new car. Tara Harding (I first read this as Tonya Harding) and two employees needed to get back to their families in Bismarck, and had patients to see Monday morning. Tara Harding and her employees were at the airport trying to get home from a work trip when a nationwide ground stop left them stranded in Charlotte, North Carolina — roughly 1,600 miles from home in Bismarck, North Dakota. She found a $48,000 solution in the form of a new Ford Bronco. https://t.co/xpP9fmCsm8 — NBC News (@NBCNews) November 16, 2026 They couldn’t find a rental car within four hours of Charlotte. They tried other ways home, including a train, bus and U-Haul. None worked. Delta Air Lines left them stranded. Harding’s mother-in-law suggested buying a car. They bought the Bronco with no money down. Harding initially planned to sell it to a dealership once they reached home. The women took turns driving and sleeping. While flights resumed at 8:15 p.m. Eastern on Friday, over 18,000 trips were cancelled and there simply weren’t seats to accommodate all passengers on later flights and it took several days to clear everyone out. There’s a calculation in buying the car, deducting depreciation, taxes and fees, financing costs and operating expenses, and selling it on the other end. There’s a very close precedent. During Southwest Airlines’ Christmas 2022 meltdown, a couple bought a $500 used car to get home, and Southwest reimbursed them. This incident wasn’t any airline’s fault. In the end, Harding abandoned the plan to resell the car. Topics on this pageFAAFederal Aviation AdministrationFord BroncoGround stopCharlotteDelta Air LinesNBC NewsNorth CarolinaNorth DakotaSouthwest Airlines+6 more More From View from the Wing

Tara Harding (I first read this as Tonya Harding) and two employees needed to get back to their families in Bismarck, and had patients to see Monday morning.

Tara Harding and her employees were at the airport trying to get home from a work trip when a nationwide ground stop left them stranded in Charlotte, North Carolina — roughly 1,600 miles from home in Bismarck, North Dakota.

She found a $48,000 solution in the form of a new Ford Bronco. https://t.co/xpP9fmCsm8

They couldn’t find a rental car within four hours of Charlotte. They tried other ways home, including a train, bus and U-Haul. None worked. Delta Air Lines left them stranded. Harding’s mother-in-law suggested buying a car.

They bought the Bronco with no money down. Harding initially planned to sell it to a dealership once they reached home. The women took turns driving and sleeping.

While flights resumed at 8:15 p.m. Eastern on Friday, over 18,000 trips were cancelled and there simply weren’t seats to accommodate all passengers on later flights and it took several days to clear everyone out.

There’s a calculation in buying the car, deducting depreciation, taxes and fees, financing costs and operating expenses, and selling it on the other end. There’s a very close precedent. During Southwest Airlines’ Christmas 2022 meltdown, a couple bought a $500 used car to get home, and Southwest reimbursed them. This incident wasn’t any airline’s fault. In the end, Harding abandoned the plan to resell the car.
