#6090. World Of Hyatt 2027 Updates: Milestone Rewards From 10 Nights, New Rewards, And More

World of Hyatt members can expect more flexibility and choice from January 1, 2027. Highlights of the update include earning Milestone Rewards sooner, a bunch of new Milestone Rewards, and more flexibility when redeeming rewards and paying for stays. There’s actually no huge catch, and the changes I learned about last night on an intimate call with the Hyatt team are genuinely member-focused.

The update follows the new Hyatt-Delta relationship, which also launched this week.

Starting January 1, 2027, World of Hyatt members will start enjoying Milestone Rewards after 10 nights stayed or 20,000 base points. That’s great news for relatively infrequent Hyatt guests (like myself), who will no longer have to stay 20 nights or earn 35,000 base points to earn their first Milestone Reward.

At 10 nights or 20,000 base points, members will be able to choose from:

Milestone Rewards will be unlocked at every ten nights, up to 150 nights.

Not only is it about to become quicker to earn Milestone Rewards, but there’ll also be new awards to choose from each level. Here are a few examples of the 20+ new rewards:

The downside of free parking becoming a Milestone Reward means that World of Hyatt members who earn Globalist from 2027 onwards will no longer enjoy it as a permanent status perk on award stays. This will be a notable downgrade to Globalists who value their parking perk.

Hyatt has published a handy new infographic with all the details.

There are also two more important Milestone Reward changes to note, both of which aren’t such positive news:

For the first time, World of Hyatt members will be able to stack multiple awards on a single stay. For example, you can use a Suite Upgrade Voucher, a Guest of Honor Award, and claim free parking, all on the same stay.

All awards will also expire after 365 of being issued. That’s great for awards that used to only last 180 days.

I think this could be my favorite update. Hyatt is enhancing its Pay My Way option to allow guests to choose how to pay for each night of a stay. As someone who struggles to rack up Hyatt points (Hyatt isn’t a transfer partner of any cards in the U.K.), this should certainly streamline booking stays for me.

The booking page will display each award applied to each individual night and provide guests with a drop-down menu to select how they’d like to pay for each night.

At a time when we’re plagued with loyalty program devaluations, these changes coming to World of Hyatt appear to be a genuinely positive slew of updates. Even when you consider some of the less favorable updates, like Globalists losing free parking and some award expiration dates being limited to 365 days, the changes will be positive overall for the vast majority of World of Hyatt members.

What do you make of these World of Hyatt changes?

#6089. A Trump–Xi–Putin Summit Could Remake the World Order

Can a triangle of the U.S., China, and Russia create a sustainable equilibrium of power, rules, and values?

From left: Russian President Vladimir Putin, President Donald Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping

NR illustration; Alexander Kazakov, Kevin Lamarque, Tingshu Wang/Reuters

The proposed Trump–Xi–Putin meeting in Shenzhen this month could become one of the most consequential diplomatic encounters since the Cold War. Whatever the three leaders might negotiate concerning Ukraine, Taiwan, trade, nuclear weapons, or artificial intelligence, its larger significance would be unmistakable: The three powers most capable of shaping the international order would be gathering not primarily to defend it but to renegotiate their positions within, or against, it.

The irony is extraordinary. Russia seeks to overturn an order from which it believes itself excluded. China seeks to reshape an order from which it has benefited enormously. The United States, which created and sustained that order, increasingly regards its maintenance as an excessive burden. The revolutionary, the reformer, and the reluctant guardian have become, in different ways, revisionists.

From left: Russian President Vladimir Putin, President Donald Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping

NR illustration; Alexander Kazakov, Kevin Lamarque, Tingshu Wang/Reuters

#6088. How Marriott Members Can Sometimes Earn Points Twice On The Same Spending

A Marriott Bonvoy member reports earning qualifying spend or extra points by charging gift card purchases to the room bill even though Marriott expressly excludes gift card purchases from the spending requirement for Ambassador status. Ambassador takes 100 qualifying nights and $23,000 in annual qualifying spend. Someone staying at inexpensive and even moderately-priced hotels can clear the nights while falling well short on dollars. If a gift card counts when you buy it, you could move future hotel spending into the current qualification year. And if the purchase and the eventual hotel stay both earn points, you’ve earned twice on the same money. An April 4 report on US Card Forum laid out some properties where this worked, and where it didn’t. Property   Reported result Ritz-Carlton Waikiki spa   Gift cards charged to the room counted toward qualifying spend. St. Regis Longboat Key   Two $1,500 cards purchased, then used at checkout; the member reports an extra round of points. Tampa EDITION   Allowed the gift-card room charge; no separate points or spending total supplied. JW Marriott Clearwater   Refused to put the purchase on the room bill. Unnamed hotel, separate commenter   A charge labeled “gc” reached the folio but earned no points. Marriott’s terms (section 4.2.b.v) exclude Marriott Gift Card purchases from Annual Qualifying Spend. The Ambassador help page says the same thing. This comes down to how the hotel records the charge and sends it to Marriott. If a gift card sale goes through as an eligible incidental, the loyalty system credits the amount without recognizing what was actually sold. A properly identified gift card entry gets excluded. There are two places this can fail: the hotel can refuse the room charge, or accept it but keep it out of the amount eligible for points and status. An employee saying “yes, we can charge that to your room” doesn’t tell you whether it will post as eligible spend. I’ve covered another example of hotel level accounting producing more Ambassador credit than you’d expect. In 2024, the Renaissance Dallas advertised a rate with 30% additional qualifying spend for $20 extra per night. That suggested how the property’s handling of a charge can affect the way Marriott credits it. If you’re a Marriott person, who’s going to spend money with them anyway (clearly an Ambassador member does) this is an interesting thing to experiment with but I also wouldn’t hit it too hard with an Ambassador account that I valued. Me, I haven’t been an Ambassador since the end of the Starwood days. #6087. Conservative firebrand Lauren Boebert ousted in Colorado

Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

The red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

A newcomer to electoral politics, she quickly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

In 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

Running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch announced he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

This year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

#6086. Lufthansa’s A380 Business Class Seat Retrofit Nearly Done, But It Isn’t Allegris

In January 2026, Lufthansa formally announced plans to retrofit its Airbus A380s with new business class seats. The first plane with new cabins entered service in April 2026, and Lufthansa had committed to retrofitting all the planes by the middle of 2027.

There’s now a positive update, as it looks like Lufthansa is running way ahead on that schedule, and all A380s should be retrofitted within the coming weeks…

Lufthansa is introducing a new business class product on its entire fleet of eight Airbus A380s. Rather interestingly, it’s only business class that’s getting new seats, while first class, premium economy, and economy, remain the same, aside from some minor upgrades (like improved inflight entertainment).

The first A380 with new interiors entered service in April 2026, and AeroRoutes flags how as of December 18, 2026, Lufthansa is exclusively showing the new business class configuration on all routes. So starting in the coming weeks, you can expect the entire A380 network to feature the new cabins.

Lufthansa A380s are based in Munich (MUC), and currently fly to Bangkok (BKK), Delhi (DEL), Los Angeles (LAX), Mumbai (BOM), San Francisco (SFO), and Washington (IAD). As you’d expect, there’s seasonal variation in the routes, though.

What’s interesting is that Lufthansa isn’t introducing its new Allegris business class on these planes, but instead, is introducing another “off the shelf” product. Specifically, the airline has opted for the Thompson Aero Vantage XL product, which is in a staggered configuration.

Each seat has direct aisle access, seat width of 58cm, and a bed length of at least two meters. Seats feature bluetooth connectivity and flexible partitions. Lufthansa is calling this “Premium XXL,” which… I’m not sure if that’s supposed to describe the seat, or if Lufthansa is taking some liberties on a new Grindr profile, somehow turning Vantage XL into Premium XXL.

As A380s are reconfigured, the business class cabin is shrinking in size by 10 seats, going from 78 seats to 68 seats. First class continues to have eight seats, premium economy continues to have 52 seats, and economy continues to have 371 seats.

It’s pretty cool to note how Lufthansa has reversed course on the A380. At the beginning of the pandemic, Lufthansa grounded its fleet of Airbus A380s, and the intent was that these planes would be retired, and would only reenter service “in the event of an unexpectedly rapid market recovery.”

With the strong recovery we’ve seen in transatlantic leisure demand, the airline made the decision to start bringing back Airbus A380s as of the summer of 2023, and eight of the initial 14 are now back in service (six of them were sold). At first, the return of the A380s was mostly described as a temporary measure, in light of delayed Boeing 777-9 deliveries. The airline didn’t commit to keeping these planes around in the long run, though that changed over time.

In recent years it has become clear that the A380 will have a long term place in Lufthansa’s fleet. Clearly this investment in the business class product reflects that.

Lufthansa of course has its new Allegris cabins, including the new Allegris business class and new Allegris first class. These cabins debuted on newly delivered Airbus A350-900s, and we’re also seeing them on newly delivered Boeing 787-9s (though without first class).

So why is Lufthansa not installing its new Allegris seats on the A380s? Well, I’d assume it comes down to a couple of factors. The biggest reason is quite straightforward — Lufthansa has had a really tough time getting its new Allegris seats certified, and these seats need to be certified on each individual aircraft. The idea is that by picking an “off the shelf” product, these seats are already certified, and therefore the airline could actually rely on getting them into service immediately.

Second of all, I imagine that given the narrower fuselage of the A380 upper deck, it might’ve required even more complicated customization to fit the new Allegris seats up there.

For once, I’d say Lufthansa made a wise decision by just picking a generic product for its A380s. I think the big mystery is why Lufthansa just didn’t do this for its other planes, to avoid this entire mess. Separately, Lufthansa is reconfiguring its Boeing 747-8s, in a complicated two-part process. Initially, we’ll see the new Allegris business class seats on the lower deck, while the same business class seats will remain on the upper deck.

Lufthansa is wrapping up the process of introducing a new business class product on its Airbus A380s. The first plane with new cabins entered service in April 2026. While the initial plan was for all planes to be reconfigured as of the middle of 2027, it looks like that project will instead wrap up by December 2026, which is amazing.

Rather than installing the new Allegris business class seats, the airline is instead installing a more generic product, the Thompson Aero Vantage XL seat, which is a significant improvement over the product you’ll otherwise find on these jets. As planes are reconfigured, business class capacity is being reduced by 10 seats, from 78 to 68.

Lufthansa sure is all over the place when it comes to modernizing its cabins. Either way, this change is good to see.

What do you make of Lufthansa’s new A380 business class?

#6085. Amex Gold Card Credits: How To Maximize $424 In Uber, Dining, Resy, & Dunkin’ Value

The American Express® Gold Card is one of the best cards for earning Membership Rewards points, and it also has an excellent welcome offer. The card is ideal for anyone who spends a lot on dining, whether at restaurants or supermarkets, and in my experience, getting approved for the card is quite easy.

The Amex Gold Card has a $325 annual fee (Rates & Fees), though the card also offers up to $424 in annual credits, which could more than offset the annual fee, not even accounting for all the other perks.

Now, a vast majority of cardmembers aren’t going to maximize all the Amex Gold Card credits, since it is a bit of a “coupon book” vibe, in terms of how the credits are issued. In this post, I’d like to take a look at the Amex Gold Card credits, including the restrictions, and how they can be redeemed.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Gold Card

With the Amex Gold Card credits, cardmembers can potentially receive statement credits with Uber, select dining establishments, Resy, and Dunkin’. The terms associated with using each of these Amex Gold credits varies, so it’s worth covering all the details. Below is a chart with the basics, and then I’ll cover all the credits in more detail.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $120 in Uber Cash annually:

What’s my take on the Amex Gold Uber Cash credit? As someone who uses both Uber and Uber Eats more than once per month, the Amex Gold Uber Cash credit benefit is basically as good as cash to me. Obviously if you don’t use Uber or Uber Eats that often, try to remember to use it earlier in the month, so you don’t forget to use it later on. That’s especially true if you have international travel plans, given that the credit only works in the United States.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $120 in dining credits annually:

What’s my take on the Amex Gold dining credit? Everyone has different spending patterns. Personally, I don’t frequently dine at any of the establishments included with the Amex Gold dining credit, though I do use Grubhub once in a while. So when I can remember to use the perk, that saves me $10 per month on those purchases.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $100 in Resy credits annually:

Let me emphasize that you don’t have to jump through hoops at a restaurant to take advantage of the Amex Gold Resy statement credit. You don’t even have to make your reservation through Resy, as long as it’s a Resy partner restaurant.

What’s my take on the Amex Gold Resy credit? If you dine out frequently and live in a decently sized city, visiting a Resy restaurant should be super easy. Personally I’m able maximize this without even trying, since I go to restaurants associated with Resy all the time.

Admittedly, this is of limited use to those in small towns, where not many restaurants may use the Resy platform. In those situations, remember to consider Resy restaurants when you’re traveling to a larger city, as that’s your best bet for maximizing that perk.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $84 in Dunkin’ credits annually:

You can maximize the Amex Gold Dunkin’ credit by spending at least $7 per month at a Dunkin’ location with your eligible card.

What’s my take on the Amex Gold Dunkin’ credit? Admittedly, this is niche, and seems like an odd fit for a premium card. Dunkin’ isn’t exactly a high-end brand, and the $7 credit seems quite random. However, I think this is easy enough to manage. It’s also worth emphasizing that as of now, simply loading your Dunkin’ account through the Dunkin’ app with $7 per month seems to trigger the credit.

Based on how I read the terms, that’s not even a fluke. The terms say the credit can’t be used for gift cards, though loading a Dunkin’ account isn’t a gift card. So as things currently stand, basically view this as an $84 annual Dunkin’ credit (which you must load monthly, but the credit as such won’t expire).

Just about any credit card with perks that are distributed throughout the year and where enrollment is required will have a significant amount of breakage. That’s only natural, and as I see it, it’s a double-edged sword. On the plus side, I view it as an opportunity for savvy consumers to get outsized value from a card. At the same time, “credit card fatigue” is a very really concept.

With that in mind, how much do I value the up to $424 in credits offered on the Amex Gold Card? Here’s my general thought process:

When all is said and done, I’d say that I value the credits on the Amex Gold Card as maybe being within $100 of the card’s annual fee, give or take. To me, that essentially puts this Membership Rewards points-earning powerhouse in line with other mid-range cards, in terms of the cost of holding onto it. Everyone’s math will differ, so crunch the numbers to decide how much value the card offers to you.

The Amex Gold Card is a product you primarily get for the excellent return it offers on everyday spending. The card has a steep annual fee, though the good news is that this can largely be offset thanks to the up to $424 in annual credits it offers. Hopefully, the above is a useful rundown of how each of the Amex Gold Card credits can be used.

The Amex Gold credits won’t be equally valuable for everyone, but if you dine at Resy restaurants and use Uber (for rides or food delivery) with any frequency, you should be able to recoup much of the annual fee thanks to the credits.

What do you make of the Amex Gold Card credits, and how much value are you able to get out of them?

#6084. Hyatt And Delta Launch Extra Points On Flights And Hotel Stays—But Standard Coach Tickets Don’t Qualify

Hyatt and Delta have launched extra points on flights and hotel stays, with airline status, lounge passes and hotel free night awards coming next year. But there’s a big restriction: even a Hyatt Globalist buying a regular Delta coach ticket earns no Hyatt points. That’s not ‘basic economy doesn’t count’ – it’s listerally standard main cabin coach that earns nothing. The companies announced their partnership in September. Now we know how the benefits actually work. This brings back some of what Hyatt members lost when American Airlines stopped reciprocal points earning at the end of 2024. But Delta excludes regular coach, gives Hyatt’s lowest elite tier half as many points, and pays hotel guests in a less valuable airline currency (SkyMiles). Who Earns Extra Points And Miles Start by linking your World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles accounts. Ongoing extra earning depends on your status: Your Status   Additional Earnings Delta Silver, Gold, Platinum or Diamond Medallion   1 SkyMile per eligible dollar spent with Hyatt, on top of Hyatt points Hyatt Discoverist   1 Hyatt point per $2 of eligible Delta premium cabin spending, on top of SkyMiles Hyatt Explorist, Globalist or Lifetime Globalist   1 Hyatt point per eligible dollar of Delta premium cabin spending, on top of SkyMiles Hyatt status qualifies you for Hyatt points on eligible Delta flights. Delta status qualifies you for SkyMiles on eligible Hyatt spending. For flights, Delta Comfort, Premium Select, First Class and Delta One qualify. Basic, Classic and Extra fare versions qualify when they’re sold in one of those cabins. So basic extra legroom coach qualifies, full fair regular coach doesn’t. . The flight earning rules also require: A Delta marketed and operated flight, with a Delta-issued ticket beginning 006. Your SkyMiles number attached before departure and Hyatt elite status when the flight is completed. A qualifying paid ticket. Eligible spending includes the base fare and airline imposed surcharges, but excludes government taxes, airport fees and amounts paid with miles. These are Hyatt bonus points. They don’t count as base points toward Hyatt status or lifetime Globalist. For hotel spending, eligible room charges, incidentals and qualifying purchases without an overnight stay can earn SkyMiles. Mr & Mrs Smith and The Venetian qualify when booked through Hyatt. Homes & Hideaways and FIND experiences are excluded. Hyatt Nights Can Earn Delta Credits, Lounge Visits And Status Beginning January 1, 2027, linked Hyatt members will have Delta options among their Milestone Rewards. These are choices, so you’ll need to compare them with the other rewards available at the same threshold. The specific awards are: Hyatt Qualification   Delta Reward Choice 20 qualifying nights or 35,000 base points   $25 Delta eCertificate 40 qualifying nights or 65,000 base points   $75 Delta eCertificate 60 qualifying nights or 100,000 base points   $100 Delta eCertificate 70, 80 or 90 qualifying nights   Two single visit Delta Sky Club passes 100 qualifying nights   Delta Gold Medallion status 150 qualifying nights   Delta Platinum Medallion status, without Choice Benefits The flight certificates and lounge passes expire one year after issuance. Each lounge pass covers one person for one visit with a qualifying same-day boarding pass (basic economy passengers excluded). The status awards are for your own account. They don’t provide anything extra if you already hold that tier or higher, and selecting the same status again doesn’t extend it. Platinum at 150 nights is potentially attractive, albeith without the Choice Benefits that normally come with that status (e.g. four Regional Upgrade Certificates). Delta Elites Can Choose Hyatt Free Nights Starting February 1, 2027, for the 2028 Medallion Year, Delta is adding: A Hyatt Category 1–4 free night as a Platinum Choice Benefit. A Hyatt Category 1–7 free night as a Diamond Choice Benefit. These aren’t extra certificates automatically handed to every Platinum and Diamond. You select one instead of another Choice Benefit. No new option to redeem SkyMiles directly for Hyatt free night certificates was announced, like we’d seen with the American partnership. Perhaps the biggest loss is Hyatt redemptions for American Airlines status for a day. Launch Bonuses Don’t Require Elite Status All linked members can participate in the launch offers: November 17–December 31, 2026: Register separately and complete a qualifying Hyatt stay to earn one additional qualifying night credit. That’s one bonus night total, not double nights for the entire stay. January 4–February 15, 2027: Complete your first eligible paid Delta Comfort-or-higher flight to earn 1,000 bonus Hyatt points. January 4–February 15, 2027: Complete your first qualifying Hyatt stay to earn 1,000 bonus SkyMiles. Paid and award stays qualify for the hotel promotions. Mr & Mrs Smith and The Venetian bookings through Hyatt qualify, while Homes & Hideaways doesn’t. The year-end stay must finish after registration and by December 31. For the January hotel offer, checkout must be by February 15. There’s also an Alila Mayakoba trip sweepstakes through November 23. Hyatt says reciprocal status challenges are coming. Is This Better Than Hyatt’s American Airlines Partnership? There are two different American partnerships to compare against. The original version, which ran through 2024, was better for everyday earning. Hyatt Discoverists earned the same one point per dollar on American airfare as Globalists, and regular coach counted. American elites earned a mile per eligible Hyatt dollar, and those miles also counted as Loyalty Points once that status system was introduced. Delta’s hotel earning has the same nominal mileage rate, but American miles are worth more. And there’s no status credit from those points. American’s final double earning terms also covered eligible FIND and Homes & Hideaways spending, both excluded here. On the flight side you’re earning Hyatt points either way, so the problem isn’t SkyMiles valuation. It’s the cabins that don’t qualify and the halved Discoverist rate. The 2025 American redesign removed double dipping and largely made members pay for partner benefits with their own points or by giving up another reward. Delta restores some actual additional earnings. The milestone comparison is mixed: Flight credits can be more useful than seat coupons. American offered two Preferred Seat coupons at 20 and 30 nights, then two Main Cabin Extra coupons at 40 and 50. Delta status starts later. American Gold was a choice at 70, 80 and 90 Hyatt nights. Delta offers lounge passes there, with its first announced status award at 100 nights. At 150 nights, Delta offers a higher tier. American’s offer topped out at Platinum. Delta Platinum is its third tier, although withholding Choice Benefits takes away a valuable part of the package. American also gave ConciergeKey members Hyatt Globalist and offered Hyatt status choices to other AAdvantage members. We’ll see what reciprocal status offers look like. It’s worth linking accounts and registering for the extra Hyatt night if there’s a stay coming up. #6082. James Talarico’s ‘Incarnational Politics’

The new senator from Texas has bad ideas about Christianity and democracy, but the press seems okay with that.

The day after the Democrats trounced the Republicans in the midterm elections, Ezra Klein of the New York Times tweeted, “One of the more exciting parts of this election — among many — is the return of a religious left.” Accompanying the enthusiastic remark was a clip from his interview earlier this year with James Talarico, the Democrat who won the Texas senatorial race. In the clip, Talarico — a Presbyterian seminarian — advocates a political attitude in which Americans recognize each other as being made in God’s image and treat each other accordingly. He calls this “an incarnational politics.”

Incarnational politics — hoo boy. The term, a nearly paradoxical union of the sacred and the profane, sounds just enough like intersectional politics to catch the attention of progressives. It also sounds like an edgy indie band that never quite made it. (“I saw Incarnational Politics open for Bad Religion in ’91.”)

#6080. Dear Tunisair: How About A Refund For My Downgrade, Please?

I’d like to think that I’m pretty understanding of airlines, and how they can fall short. The airline industry is incredibly complex and low margin, and sometimes consumers have unrealistically high expectations, while not acknowledging the real cost and challenges of running an airline. Buying a ticket on a flight is more like buying a ticket on Amtrak than buying a night at a Four Seasons, and you should adjust expectations accordingly.

At the same time, sometimes there are situations where airlines act in a way that feels to me a little like theft. Readers often share these stories with me, and I write about them when I can. Now I’d like to share my own story…

Several weeks ago, I booked a ticket on Tunisair in business class from Tunis (TUN) to Marseille (MRS). A few days before the flight I received an email from Tunisair informing me that I had been downgraded. As it turns out, it was because my flight was swapped to a wet leased plane, in an all-economy layout.

The email informed me of this change without actually acknowledging it was a downgrade. Instead, the email was in French, and it translated to “we are writing to inform you that your flight reservation has undergone changes.” And the only reference to the downgrade was that the fare class only showed as being “Y,” which obviously isn’t business class.

There was zero other proactive communication from the airline about the incident, and I flew the flight in economy. The airline of course acted as if nothing happened, and there was no mention of how to request downgrade compensation, or anything like that.

After the flight, I submitted a request with customer service, asking for a refund for the fare difference. Making that request was a challenge in and of itself, because the customer service form is in French, and is not at all intuitive.

But anyway, it has been weeks, and I haven’t heard back. I’m a bit conflicted here. I try not to abuse credit card disputes, but you typically only have 60 days to file a dispute. So am I at the point where I should just file a dispute, or how would one handle that?

As I said above, I try to be pretty understanding of airlines, and recognize how many different scenarios there are. Just in terms of doing business ethically, I do feel like there should be a proactive refund offer if the airline is informing you in advance that you won’t be getting the product that you paid for. I mean, if you can inform me that I’ve been downgraded, you can also process some sort of a refund.

We’ve become desensitized to this kind of service level with airlines, but I’m trying to come up with a comparison. I guess it would be like buying premium tickets to a sporting event, being informed in advance that you’ll be given worse seats, and then customer service just not responding to you for weeks on end.

If you managed to take my money, surely you can also manage to give it back if you can’t give me the thing I paid for, no?

Tunisair informed me days before a flight that I had been downgraded (as it turns out, due to an aircraft swap), though there was no offer a refund for a fare difference, or anything. Weeks ago I sent an email to customer service asking for a refund for the fare difference, but I haven’t heard back.

It just strikes me as really unethical to take someone’s money for an experience you’re not going to offer, and then not have a way to get a refund in a reasonable timeframe. I know airlines hate when people file credit card disputes, but when you’re approaching the 60-day mark with no response, what is one supposed to do?

Am I the only one who thinks it’s ridiculous to proactively downgrade a customer, but then make getting a refund such a runaround?

#6079. Chase Adds Qantas And Cathay Pacific Transfers—More Access To Premium Award Seats

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Chase is adding Qantas and Cathay Pacific as 1:1 transfer partners on November 18. For me, the biggest value is access to business and first class award seats that these airlines don’t make available to members of other frequent flyer programs.

These are Chase’s first new airline transfer partners in more than five years. And they’re an unambiguously positive addition, even if neither becomes the program most cardmembers use most often.

Eligible cards include Chase Sapphire Reserve, Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve for Business, Ink Business Preferred and J.P. Morgan Reserve. Both new partners transfer at 1:1. Hyatt transfers are now less generous for Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred: 4 Chase points become 3 Hyatt points, while the Reserve cards retain 1:1. That distinction doesn’t apply to these new airline partners. Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees) is a strong card for actual spending, with 4 points per dollar on flights and hotels booked directly and 3 points per dollar on dining. Adding more transfer partners makes the value of those points even greater. Why I Want Qantas Points Chase already had ways to book oneworld flights through programs like British Airways and Iberia. But being able to book an airline doesn’t mean having access to all of its award seats. Airlines increasingly keep more of their premium cabin availability for their own members. As I explained when Rove added Qantas transfers, Qantas offers its members award space that American AAdvantage, Alaska and British Airways members can’t book. I have family in Australia and have had real success finding Qantas business class awards when there’s flexibility over the U.S. gateway and travel date. I’ll set alerts across several flights rather than insist on one. Some flight between Australia and the U.S. will inevitably open up with a couple of business class awards, usually around 60 days out. Qantas can also be useful for Emirates redemptions. I’d generally rather book the same available Emirates business class seat through Copa ConnectMiles, though. Copa charges 80,000 miles one way between the U.S. and Dubai in business class without fuel surcharges. And Qantas is no longer an unrestricted way around Emirates’ first class award limits. Booking Emirates first class with Qantas points requires Qantas Silver status or higher, and passengers must be at least nine years old. Cathay Offers More Award Space And Lower British Airways Surcharges Cathay Pacific is similar. Its own members get access to far more premium cabin award space than members of partner programs. Asia Miles prices can be high, though. I also like Asia Miles for reducing fuel surcharges on British Airways awards, particularly compared with booking through American AAdvantage. It’s also notable that Chase’s Cathay transfer rate is better than American Express’s. American Express transfers 1,000 Membership Rewards points to just 800 Asia Miles. An award requiring 100,000 Asia Miles takes 100,000 Chase points versus 125,000 Amex points (without transfer bonus). American Express, Citi, Capital One and Rove already partner with both Qantas and Cathay. Chase is catching up with these. I wouldn’t transfer points just because these options have been added. Chase Is Finally Adding Airline Partners Again Chase’s last new transfer partner was Wyndham Rewards in February 2026. Its last new airline partner was Air Canada Aeroplan on August 3, 2021. I welcomed Wyndham because it showed Chase was building out Ultimate Rewards, even though I had little interest in transferring points there. Qantas and Cathay are programs I can see myself using. They bring Chase to 12 airline transfer programs and four hotel programs. I also wonder whether these relationships could lead to more Points Boost opportunities. With Points Boost, Chase can use discounts it negotiates on paid tickets to offer more value per point through its travel portal. More airline relationships could help them offer more flights, more dates, or better redemption values. Qantas has already appeared in Points Boost, and American Airlines has participated without being a Chase transfer partner. But I’d love to see deeper relationships produce more opportunities to redeem at 2 cents per point for premium cabin tickets in the future. #6078. Park Hyatt Brisbane Opening 2031, As Brand’s Fourth Australia Hotel

Hyatt will bring its luxury Park Hyatt brand to Brisbane, Australia. More Park Hyatt locations are always a good thing, but… well, let’s cover the details first.

Hyatt has announced plans for the Park Hyatt Brisbane, marking the brand’s debut in Queensland. The hotel is expected to open in 2031, and will be located on the shores of the Brisbane River, at the western edge of the city’s central business district.

The hotel will occupy the top floors of one of the two towers of the 309 North Quay, a mixed-use development also containing luxury homes and retail outlets. For what it’s worth, the two buildings will have 51 floors and 56 floors. The hotel will have 201 guest rooms and suites, offering views of the river and skyline, along with 50 serviced apartments, for extended residence.

There are no additional details about the property yet. I do appreciate that the hotel will at least be at the top of a building, as that should make for some very nice views (I hate when hotels are part of tall buildings, but then take up the bottom floors, as that’s becoming increasingly common).

While a 2031 opening is expected, I would definitely not count on that timeline sticking. Ground hasn’t even broken on this development, and these kinds of mixed-use developments tend to struggle with sticking to their planned timeline.

Here’s how Tamara Lohan, Hyatt’s Global Brand Leader for Luxury, describes this:

“The Park Hyatt calling cards have always been iconic design and extraordinary addresses. Brisbane has the confidence and growing global pull to make it a natural home for the brand. When it opens, Park Hyatt Brisbane will become the fifth Park Hyatt hotel in the Pacific, joining hotels in Sydney, Melbourne, Canberra and Auckland, and a deliberate next step in growing the brand in the right places.”

There are no renderings of the property yet, beyond the below one of the overall 309 North Quay development.

This will be the fourth Park Hyatt property in Australia, and the fifth in the South Pacific, complementing the properties in Auckland, Canberra, Melbourne, and Sydney. I don’t have the slightest clue what’s going on with the Canberra property, as my understanding is that it’s not up to Park Hyatt standards, so it’s marketed as “Hyatt Hotel Canberra – A Park Hyatt Hotel.” So it is a Park Hyatt, or is it not a Park Hyatt?

World of Hyatt is my favorite major hotel loyalty program (though the lead is narrowing as of late), and Park Hyatt is probably my favorite Hyatt brand. 15 years ago, the brand got me really excited, because it had some really spectacular properties. But it just feels like the brand is sort of losing steam, especially when you compare the difference in trajectory between Park Hyatt and Waldorf Astoria. My frustration with Park Hyatt comes down to two things.

First, the brand just seemingly can’t pick up many “flagship” properties, or at least can’t maintain them. Look at the world’s biggest business markets and most iconic cities — we’re talking Hong Kong, London, New York, Paris, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, etc. There are no Park Hyatts in places like Hong Kong or Singapore, and the ones that have historically been pretty iconic just fall short of actually being the top properties in their cities:

The area where Park Hyatt has been doing well in recent times is in secondary cities, at least in comparison to the above. And this isn’t meant to be shade — I’d much rather hang out in Auckland or Kuala Lumpur than in London or New York (take your pitchforks elsewhere!), but there’s no denying that any true luxury hotel brand wants to have world class properties in those primary cities.

I just feel like as of late, Waldorf Astoria’s trajectory has been way more impressive than Park Hyatt’s, and I’m not sure what exactly is driving that. I feel like owners just aren’t as into developing Park Hyatts as they used to be. Is there a single Park Hyatt in the pipeline where I think “oh, this is going to be a best-in-class property in a major market?” I can’t think of any…

The Park Hyatt brand is coming to Brisbane, Australia, with a hotel expected to open in 2031. The 201-key property will be located on the top floors of a mixed-use development, which will also contain apartments and retail.

It’s cool to see more Park Hyatts in the pipeline, and I don’t want to knock the brand for expanding to more markets. I’m just disappointed that the Park Hyatt brand can’t pick up any steam in the biggest cities, in terms of delivering an actually competitive experience.

What do you make of plans for the Park Hyatt Brisbane?

#6077. World Of Hyatt Status Revamps For 2027—Award Stacking And New Benefit Choices, But Cuts Come Also

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Hyatt will finally let members combine a free night certificate with a confirmed suite upgrade starting January 1, 2027. I’ve wanted that for years. They’re also extending milestone free night certificates from 180 days to a year, and adding rewards after just 10 qualifying nights.

This isn’t an across the board improvement. Suite upgrades will expire sooner. The suite upgrade choice at 50 nights gets cut in half. And My Hyatt Concierge becomes something you select alongside other rewards, rather than something everyone automatically receives at 60 nights. Free parking will no longer be an automatic benefit on award stays for Globalists.

When I covered Hyatt’s last major status benefit refresh in November 2023, I liked it overall. They made awards transferable, added choices, and let members try Globalist benefits before earning Globalist. Guest of Honor became limited, but the Milestone Rewards themselves mostly got better.

This time there are new and better options. I genuinely like a lot of the choices, but there are real tradeoffs. Hyatt is pitching the changes as more choice and flexibility, based on listening to members. That’s actually fair for much of this, though I don’t think members told them what they really wanted was for suite upgrade to expire up to a year earlier.

Hyatt will allow members to combine eligible awards on the same reservation, including Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards and the new Free Parking Awards. This fixes one of the problems I’ve been complaining about for years. A free night certificate is something you often want to use on a special leisure stay. That’s also when a suite may matter most, especially traveling with family. When I didn’t want to use a free night certificate was a work trip by myself. Free night awards had a lot less value to me because I had to give up a confirmed suite to use them. But being able to use the two awards together makes both more valuable. Combining Guest of Honor with a suite upgrade is useful, too. You can give someone Globalist treatment and confirm their suite ahead of time, rather than leaving the room upgrade to availability when they arrive. Hyatt also promises an enhanced Pay My Way experience, letting members mix awards, points, cash and Points + Cash by night. Online selection, gifting and redemption will be available for eligible awards. Pay My Way and stacking, by the way, really do all work together. Hyatt offers me this illustration, Let’s say a member is making a three night booking. Assuming both the Standard Suite was available for the duration, and there is award inventory available on the selected dates (just like today) – yes, a member could apply a Suite Upgrade Award to the whole stay, a Free Parking award to the whole stay, a Guest of Honor Award to the whole stay, and then pay for the reservation using points on one night, a promotional Free Night Award on another night, and cash on the third night.

Let’s say a member is making a three night booking. Assuming both the Standard Suite was available for the duration, and there is award inventory available on the selected dates (just like today) – yes, a member could apply a Suite Upgrade Award to the whole stay, a Free Parking award to the whole stay, a Guest of Honor Award to the whole stay, and then pay for the reservation using points on one night, a promotional Free Night Award on another night, and cash on the third night.

Milestone Rewards currently begin at 20 qualifying nights. Next year they’ll start at 10 nights or 20,000 base points. Here’s the new chart through 50 nights. Qualifying nights / base points   What you receive 10 / 20,000   Choose one: 1 qualifying night credit, $25 FIND experience credit, or $30 Inclusive Collection spa credit. 20 / 35,000   Choose one: 2 qualifying night credits, $30 spa credit, $25 Delta certificate, 2K Next Stay Award, or 2 Club Access Awards. 30 / 50,000   Choose 10,000 bonus points or a Category 1–4 free night. Also choose one: 2 qualifying night credits, $30 spa credit, $25 Delta certificate, 2K Next Stay Award, or 2 Club Access Awards. 40 / 65,000   Receive 1 Guest of Honor Award. Also choose one: 5 qualifying night credits, $200 Thompson Hotels credit, $75 Delta certificate, 5,000 points, or 1 Suite Upgrade Award. 50 / 80,000   Choose one: $200 Thompson Hotels credit, $75 Delta certificate, 5,000 points, or 1 Suite Upgrade Award. The qualifying night choices add up to 10 nights: one at the first milestone, two at the next, two at 30 nights and five at 40 nights. These count toward both status and Milestone Rewards. That creates a path to Globalist with 50 qualifying nights from other sources, if you select all four night rewards. The requirement remains 60, but 10 can come from these choices. And you earn qualifying nights with the The World Of Hyatt Credit Card (See rates and fees) too – 5 qualifying night credits every year and 2 qualifying night every time you spend $5,000 on the card. The 30 night option to take 10,000 points instead of a Category 1–4 certificate is useful for someone who struggles to use the certificate. A good Category 4 redemption can be worth more, and the certificate will become easier to use with the longer expiration and ability to add a suite upgrade. One Fewer Suite Upgrade, And A Choice About Your Concierge The reduction at 50 nights is easy to miss. The current choice is two Suite Upgrade Awards. The new chart offers one. At 60 nights or 100,000 base points, members will receive: 2 Guest of Honor Awards. A choice of free nights: 2 Category 1–4 awards or 1 Category 1–7 award. Two selections from this menu: 7,500 bonus points, a Free Parking Award, a $100 Delta certificate, 2 Suite Upgrade Awards, or My Hyatt Concierge. You can still select the two suite upgrades and concierge access, keeping the existing 60 night package. But if you want points or parking, something else has to go. And you can’t make the same two choices at 60 nights – you can’t have four upgrades, 15,000 points or two parking awards. You don’t have o select all of your awards at once, though you do have to make these two selections at the same time. Hyatt explains to me that you’ll still have 90 days to make your choices, and: In milestones where there are separate choices, such as 30 nights, the member can make those choices at different points within the 90 day selection window (e.g., could choose the Free Night Award one day, and the HIC Spa credit on a different day.) At 60 nights, the member can choose their free night award choice on a different day from the other selection, but the two selections within “Choose Two” must be made together at the same time. I do plan to keep the concierge benefit, even though mine has never been very responsive. I won’t give up the ability to email someone to address issues. I just wish I would hear back more quickly, and didn’t need to follow up so often. Maybe that’s actually coming? Hyatt tells me they do plan greater investment in the concierge program: [B]y shifting to a choice, we will be able to further invest in My Hyatt Concierge and deliver even more proactive and personalized care. We will share more when available.

And you can’t make the same two choices at 60 nights – you can’t have four upgrades, 15,000 points or two parking awards. You don’t have o select all of your awards at once, though you do have to make these two selections at the same time. Hyatt explains to me that you’ll still have 90 days to make your choices, and:

In milestones where there are separate choices, such as 30 nights, the member can make those choices at different points within the 90 day selection window (e.g., could choose the Free Night Award one day, and the HIC Spa credit on a different day.) At 60 nights, the member can choose their free night award choice on a different day from the other selection, but the two selections within “Choose Two” must be made together at the same time.

I do plan to keep the concierge benefit, even though mine has never been very responsive. I won’t give up the ability to email someone to address issues. I just wish I would hear back more quickly, and didn’t need to follow up so often. Maybe that’s actually coming? Hyatt tells me they do plan greater investment in the concierge program:

[B]y shifting to a choice, we will be able to further invest in My Hyatt Concierge and deliver even more proactive and personalized care. We will share more when available.

As before, lifetime Globalists retain their concierge without having to stay 60 nights.

The new parking award covers a qualifying paid or award stay of up to seven nights, and can be gifted. It appears among the choices at 60, 70, 80 and 90 nights. However it’s no longer simply a benefit for Globalists redeeming points for free nights. I wrote in that Hyatt was surveying turning automatic benefits into awards you could choose and they’ve done that with this one. The benefit is no longer unlimited It comes with a tradeoff – the benefit is instead of something else And you have to plan ahead, one more thing to track and manage, rather than something that’s just ‘taken care of’ in recognition of your loyalty. Hyatt explains the decision to me as, [T]his decision was made as 70% of Globalists did not use the free parking benefit in 2025; 95% used it 4 times or less, and moving this to a choice allowed the program to retain it for members who value it and introduce other exciting new awards like the $200 Thompson Hotels Credit and the $500 Premium Suite Credit. If the benefit wasn’t being used, it actually wasn’t that expensive to offer! And not using it regularly doesn’t mean the option isn’t valued. It may not have been the most valuable benefit of Globalist for most people, but I wouldn’t personally make the tradeoff (in fairness, I’m someone that did use and get value from it). Of course, a parking award will be eligible for use a paid stay while it previously was only available on points. However, at 70, 80 or 90 nights where you can claim it you’re passing up 10,000 points or a suite upgrade to select it. A Year To Use Every Award Is Both An Improvement And A Cut Hyatt’s release presents the new expiration policy as giving members extra time. That’s true for some awards, but the effect runs in both directions. Hyatt tells me, For all awards issued on January 1, 2027 or later, expiration dates will be 365 days from the date of issuance. Milestone free night awards that currently expire after 180 days will get substantially more time. But suite upgrades, ordinary Milestone Guest of Honor awards and club access awards currently have much longer lives, generally through the end of the year earned plus another 14 months under Hyatt’s existing rules. A suite upgrade selected January 1, 2026 remained valid through February 2028. Under a 365 day rule, the same issuance date would produce a January 1, 2027 expiration. That’s more than a year of usefulness gone. Shortening the window makes it harder to hold upgrades for a major trip, to book far ahead, or to save awards from a heavy travel year for a quieter one. Note that this change applies to Milestone Rewards earned starting in 2027. So any that you earn at the end of 2026, and redeem in 2027, follow the old rules. Hyatt confirms, Only awards earned and selected after January 1, 2027 follow the new 365 expiration from issuance. So, a 2026 award (even if selected in 2027) would carry the current 2026 expiration rules. More Free Night Choices And Delta Status At Higher Milestones Here’s the rest of the 2027 chart: Qualifying nights   What you receive 70, 80 and 90, at each milestone   1 Guest of Honor Award, plus choose one: a Free Parking Award, 2 single visit Delta Sky Club passes, 10,000 points, or 1 Suite Upgrade Award. 100   Choose 1 Category 1–7 night, 2 Category 1–4 nights, or a $500 premium suite credit. Also choose one: Delta Gold Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. 110, 120, 130 and 140, at each milestone   1 Guest of Honor Award, plus choose one: Delta Gold Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. 150   Choose 2 Category 1–7 nights or an Ultimate Free Night Award. Also choose one: Delta Platinum Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. The Ultimate Free Night at 150 nights isn’t going away. The two Category 1–7 nights are an alternative. Someone who wants two nights at less expensive hotels can choose those, while someone planning one especially expensive night can retain the Ultimate award, which covers participating Category 1–8 hotels, Category A–F all-inclusives and Miraval. The new hotel credits are more restrictive than points: $30 Inclusive Collection spa credit: for spa treatments at participating all-inclusive resorts. $200 Thompson Hotels credit: toward an eligible paid stay. $500 premium suite credit: toward an eligible paid premium suite stay of at least two nights. I’ve wanted a way to use two suite upgrades to confirm a premium suite. A discount on buying a premium suite isn’t as attractive to me. But there are times I might use it. Delta Gold starting at 100 nights and Platinum at 150 nights are interesting choices for someone who flies Delta without status. I still preferred the American partnership. The ability to redeem Hyatt points for American status for a trip was useful for people who didn’t have American status. And the earlier version earned American miles on Hyatt stays. I’d rather earn those than Delta miles. FIND credits are being pared back sharply. The $25 choices at 20 and 30 nights disappear, as do $150 choices at 40 and 50 nights and $300 choices at 70, 80 and 90. A $25 FIND choice appears at the new 10 night milestone. What Hyatt Gets From These Changes The strongest improvements are award stacking, more time to use free night certificates, an earlier first reward, and choices that let members avoid awards they won’t use. A member who doesn’t value concierge access can get something else, while someone who prefers two less expensive hotel nights can choose them. I expect members approaching Globalist will like the qualifying night choices. People who lose free night certificates to expiration should come out ahead, too. Existing Globalists who use all their suite upgrades, plan trips far ahead, or regularly choose FIND experiences have more to lose. Hyatt also gets more ways to influence where members spend. A Thompson credit encourages a paid Thompson stay. A spa credit encourages a treatment that may cost much more than the credit. The premium suite credit encourages someone to buy a room they might otherwise try to upgrade into. Shorter suite award validity should leave fewer outstanding upgrades available for future use. Making concierge elective lets members reveal whether they value the service more than points or another reward. And offering status credits makes the next milestone feel closer, encouraging someone with a modest number of Hyatt nights to keep going. For me, being able to confirm a suite on a free night certificate is the biggest improvement. I care much more about that than a spa coupon. There really is more choice and the ability to earn status faster with these changes. Stacking and combining rewards is great. So is longer expiration of free night awards, though sadly at the cost of shorter expiration for suite upgrade awards. The most consequential change for me might be something that isn’t really being announced. If changing My Hyatt Concierge to a choice benefit really does entail greater investment in the program, it would make the experience far more premium and secure even greater loyalty. Making concierge elective lets members reveal whether they value the service more than points or another reward. And offering status credits makes the next milestone feel closer, encouraging someone with a modest number of Hyatt nights to keep going. For me, being able to confirm a suite on a free night certificate is the biggest improvement. I care much more about that than a spa coupon. There really is more choice and the ability to earn status faster with these changes. Stacking and combining rewards is great. So is longer expiration of free night awards, though sadly at the cost of shorter expiration for suite upgrade awards. The most consequential change for me might be something that isn’t really being announced. If changing My Hyatt Concierge to a choice benefit really does entail greater investment in the program, it would make the experience far more premium and secure even greater loyalty. Topics on this pageHyattLoyalty programWorld Of HyattDelta Air Lines+1 more More From View from the Wing

The strongest improvements are award stacking, more time to use free night certificates, an earlier first reward, and choices that let members avoid awards they won’t use. A member who doesn’t value concierge access can get something else, while someone who prefers two less expensive hotel nights can choose them.

I expect members approaching Globalist will like the qualifying night choices. People who lose free night certificates to expiration should come out ahead, too. Existing Globalists who use all their suite upgrades, plan trips far ahead, or regularly choose FIND experiences have more to lose.

Hyatt also gets more ways to influence where members spend. A Thompson credit encourages a paid Thompson stay. A spa credit encourages a treatment that may cost much more than the credit. The premium suite credit encourages someone to buy a room they might otherwise try to upgrade into.

Shorter suite award validity should leave fewer outstanding upgrades available for future use. Making concierge elective lets members reveal whether they value the service more than points or another reward. And offering status credits makes the next milestone feel closer, encouraging someone with a modest number of Hyatt nights to keep going.

For me, being able to confirm a suite on a free night certificate is the biggest improvement. I care much more about that than a spa coupon.

There really is more choice and the ability to earn status faster with these changes. Stacking and combining rewards is great. So is longer expiration of free night awards, though sadly at the cost of shorter expiration for suite upgrade awards.

The most consequential change for me might be something that isn’t really being announced. If changing My Hyatt Concierge to a choice benefit really does entail greater investment in the program, it would make the experience far more premium and secure even greater loyalty.

Hyatt’s concierge service for globalists is generally useless.

If I’m going a resort, I’m not arriving with a car. Same for if I’m redeeming points to stay at the Park Hyatt in Paris or wherever. In short, it’s a way to extract a portion of the revenue lost from waived resort or destination fees from a segment of guests who arrive with a car and want to park it at the hotel.

#6076. We Need a Better GOP

President Donald Trump attends the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, September 9, 2026.

The old Republican establishment could be out of touch, unimaginative, and too comfortable with revolving-door practices that enriched former officeholders and staffers, among other failings.

Beginning in 2016, Donald Trump burned this establishment to the ground and created a new one that has its own myriad deficiencies, some of which echo the failings of yore; the extremely online elements of today’s establishment, for instance, have found a whole new way to be out of touch.

We say this not to pine for yesterday’s establishment — parties never go back, only forward — but to make the point that every party elite reaches its point of exhaustion, and that’s where the Trump establishment is now.

There is a robust intramural argument on the right over how to interpret the historic loss in the midterms. We have our own views, but the most elemental need is a better GOP — one that is not beholden to the will of one man, doesn’t tolerate corruption, insists on strict adherence to the rule of law, encourages Congress to take up its allotted role in our constitutional system, rewards policy entrepreneurship on the part of officeholders, and focuses on results rather than performative provocations.

It’s possible to imagine any number of people leading such a national party, and it could have different ideological colorations depending on that leader and underlying circumstances. All that is TBD and should be a matter of fierce debate and competition. But unless the party moves beyond today’s establishment and renews itself, it risks subsequent devastating votes of no confidence from the American public.

Consider the issue of corruption, which was one of the biggest concerns of voters in the midterms. It is one thing for a party to suffer politically in the course of making progress on an important priority — say, stepped-up immigration enforcement. It is another to suffer from the perception — and, sadly, the reality — that politically connected people are engaged in untoward schemes for their own enrichment. The former is an inevitable political trade-off; the latter is a party’s elite feasting on its power and connections with no heed to the consequences for the larger cause.

President Trump, who has an overawing dominance over the party, is the source of many of the GOP’s current discontents. His influence is not going to drastically diminish anytime soon, and we know that many good Republicans have considered him better than the alternative, or have thrilled to his no-holds-barred assaults on the left. However one evaluates the Trump phenomenon, though, attempts to rely on the tropes that fueled his rise beginning in 2016, or ape his political style, will almost certainly fail — for the simple reasons that times change and Trump’s persona is not replicable.

The GOP could do much worse than look to the states, where Republican governors and legislators have cut taxes, restrained spending, pared back regulations, protected unborn children, and pursued reforms of schooling and housing. One reason that Florida constituted high ground beyond the reach of the blue wave is that it has been so well governed for so long, and it has had a series of reformist Republican governors focused on results.

At the national level, the GOP obviously needs a cost-of-living agenda that addresses high costs in health care, medicine, and education, and there’s much work that’s been done on these issues at the state level and among conservative policy thinkers. But arriving at a coherent agenda will require a seriousness of purpose and substantive focus that have been lacking for years now. That doesn’t mean the party should be dull and conventional — much can be learned from Trump’s zest for combat and vivid political branding — but it needs to recover a sense of institutional self-respect.

The new establishment, via President Trump, has worked its way back around to what were widely considered weaknesses of the old one. Republicans were once determined to make another push for amnesty after every election loss, and now, the president has floated that idea in response to the Democratic midterm victory; Republicans were once too soft on China, and Trump has been notably conciliatory in his second term; the GOP once talked a good game on deficit spending but didn’t do nearly enough to curtail it, while we are now adding to the debt hand over fist during a time of economic expansion and relative peace; the Tom DeLay–led Republican House was much too cozy with lobbyists, but prior GOP ethical lapses have been eclipsed over the past two years.

The old establishment had reached its expiration date and, regardless, isn’t coming back, while the current establishment is harmful to the party’s image and interests and an obstacle to change.

As Lincoln said, it is a time to think anew and act anew. The GOP desperately needs something fresh and different, with ideas and policies designed to meet the challenges of the day.

#6075. Fun & Creative Airline Callsigns, From Shamrock To Starwalker

Here’s a fun topic for aviation geeks (so if you’re not one, feel free to skip this post)…

When pilots and air traffic controllers communicate, they have a callsign that they use to be identified.

In general aviation, that callsign is just the aircraft’s registration code, so it’s always the same for a particular aircraft. For example, if the plane has the registration code N111PG, it would be spoken as “November One One One Papa Golf.”

Meanwhile for commercial aircraft, the callsign consists of a company identifier plus the flight number. In some cases that company identifier is simply the company’s name, while in other cases, a different callsign is used. For example, for American, Delta, and United, the company identifier is simply the airline name, so American flight 100 would be spoken as “American 100.”

In some situations, airlines choose callsigns that are different from the company name, and this can be for a variety of reasons. Callsigns need to be approved by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), with some important considerations:

While most airlines simply use their name as their callsign, there are also some airlines that don’t, and there are some names that I find to be particularly fun. In this post, I’d like to share my favorite airline callsigns, with a little backstory on how they were chosen (as I understand it). In no particular order…

Aer Lingus’ callsign is “Shamrock,” and that’s because the shamrock is the national symbol of Ireland. It’s a key part of the airline’s corporate identity, down to the shamrock being featured on the tails of Aer Lingus planes.

British Airways’ callsign is “Speedbird,” and I’d argue it’s perhaps the most iconic callsign out there. The origin of this dates back to British Airways’ predecessor, Imperial Airways, which used the stylized bird logo. British Airways has been using the callsign since it was founded in 1974 (as a combination of predecessors).

While this is of course a creative callsign, it has a practical use as well. “British Airways” would’ve been too long of a callsign, and “British” would’ve likely been too generic. For example, British Midland (which ended up being merged into British Airways) used “Midland” as its callsign, to avoid confusion.

Republic Airways’ callsign is “Brickyard,” and it’s probably the coolest callsign you’ll find at an airline in the United States. The callsign is a tribute to the company’s headquarters in Indianapolis, also home to the Indianapolis Motor Speedway. The course was initially paved with three million bricks, and nicknamed “The Brickyard.”

For those not familiar, Republic operates flights on behalf of the regional subsidiaries of the major US carriers, so this is among the most common callsigns you’ll hear on air traffic control frequencies in the US.

PSA Airlines’ callsign is “Blue Streak,” and after Republic, it’s probably the coolest callsign you’ll find at an airline in the United States. The story behind this callsign is definitely a blast from the past. In the 1980s, PSA’s predecessor was Jetstream International Airlines, and it operated commuter flights as a Piedmont Commuter feeder carrier.

The carrier’s planes had a white fuselage with a prominent blue stripe along it, intended to match Piedmont Airlines’ livery, and that’s where it all started.

For those not familiar, PSA operates flights on behalf of the regional subsidiaries of the major US carriers, so this is also a very common callsign that you’ll hear. Given the lack of blue stripes nowadays, the callsign does tend to cause some confusion!

China Airlines’ callsign is “Dynasty.” It’s my understanding that the Taiwan-based carrier had to choose a non-obvious callsign both to avoid confusion (given the number of airlines with “China” in their name), and also with the intent of differentiating it from mainland China.

So, where did the dynasty term come from? China Airlines uses this branding pretty widely, with its frequent flyer program even being named Dynasty Flyer, and it’s intended to reflect the history of Taiwan.

Starlux Airlines’ callsign is “Starwalker.” The reason is because the “Starlux” callsign was already taken by Comlux Aruba, a tiny charter airline, before the Taiwanese airline was founded. Now, don’t ask me why Comlux Aruba has “Starlux” as its callsign, though!

The reason Starlux ended up with “Starwalker” is presumably because the company’s founder is a huge Star Wars fan, which is why many things about the airline have space branding. He’s also of course a huge aviation geek, and operates flights as a captain!

South African Airways’ callsign is “Springbok.” The reason is because “South African” would be too long of a callsign, so they selected the springbok, which is the national animal of South Africa. The carrier has also used this in its branding over the years. For example, back in the 1950s, the airline used “Springbok Service” to describe its long haul, flagship flights.

Atlas Air’s callsign is “Giant.” Huh, say what? For those not familiar, Atlas Air is a cargo and charter airline, and while it doesn’t operate regularly scheduled commercial flights, it is a big operation.

The callsign is presumably a reflection of the company’s name coming from Greek mythology, where “Atlas” was a titan of great strength, so that may also explain the “giant” callsign. Now, it’s worth mentioning that Atlas also flies some pretty “giant” planes, as the world’s largest Boeing 747 operator, but I don’t think that’s the primary motivation.

Kalitta Air’s callsign is “Connie.” For those not familiar, Kalitta Air is a cargo airline with a few dozen planes (most of which are Boeing 747s!). The callsign is named after the company’s founder, Conrad “Connie” Kalitta, who started the airline back in 1967, as Connie Kalitta Services.

European Air Transport’s callsign is “Postman.” For context, this is one of DHL’s European subsidiaries operating cargo flights, so it’s a pretty fitting callsign, eh?

Airlines have callsigns that they use to communicate with air traffic control. While most airlines simply use their name as their callsign, that’s not always the case. In some situations a different name has to be chosen for practical reasons, while in some cases airlines want to get creative. I love when airlines have some fun with this, so I figured it was worth a post.

One that brings a chuckle to me is IFLY, the callsign of IndiGo, India’s largest airline (also the name of its training academy) — mildly funny because I-Fly Airlines is a Russian charter airline with a distinctive blue and gold livery. #6074. Former Washington Rep. Jim McDermott dies at 89

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call)

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.

In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

“Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”

When McDermott announced his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”

Born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

He attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against new sanctions on Iran.

Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a new life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

“I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”

As he said, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

Then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

“The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he said in a statement at the time.

McDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

“Jim McDermott was as big as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”
