#6073. Demand For $1,589 In Rental Car Damage Dropped After Pointing Out Illegal Fees

Sixt demanded $1,589 from a customer for splatter and scuffs on a rental car, including nearly $500 in illegal fees. The customer disputed the claim, complained to consumer agencies, and says it went to collections anyway. The bill disappeared once the practice came under scrutiny. Christopher Nienhuis, a Colorado resident, rented a Buick at Milwaukee airport in October while visiting Marquette University. Days after returning it, he received a damage bill for black splatter around the license plate and near the tires, along with white scuffing around the rear windshield. He says he didn’t cause the damage and that the black material could simply be washed off. Sixt dropped the claim a week after being contacted by a news reporter. Four Renters Were Billed Fees Wisconsin Doesn’t Allow Four customers with disputed claims from the same airport location complained of illegal charges. Todd Lofgren: $6,265 for “graffiti.” He described white specks near a tire and along the bumper. The photos and invoice were dated August 18, three days after he returned the car. The bill included $1,161 in prohibited fees. Sixt dropped it September 28 after he challenged it through multiple channels. Brenda Bassett: nearly $600 for a dent already documented. The rear dent was listed in her rental agreement before she took the 2025 Toyota. About $137 consisted of diminished value and appraisal fees. A September 15 letter came from Strala Group, which handles claims for Sixt. The claim was dropped. Autumn Wojciechowski: $872 for a scratch underneath the car. She’d photographed the vehicle before driving away, but not its underside. Nearly $200 of her October 2025 damage invoice consisted of prohibited fees. This claim was dropped, too. All four claims have been withdrawn. Wisconsin law limits damage liability to reasonable repair costs, reflecting discounts available to the rental company, or the vehicle’s value before the damage, whichever is lower. Loss of use, administrative charges and appraisal fees are prohibited. Diminished value charges (loss in resale value) aren’t allowed either. Sixt Already Settled A Damage Billing Lawsuit Sixt’s 2025 damage billing settlement addressed allegations involving estimated repairs, diminished value, loss of use and administrative charges. The $11 million package included about $2.87 million in potential refunds and $6.6 million in abandoned collection claims, along with legal and administrative costs. The incentives are lousy. A customer can pay to make a collection demand go away, turn it over to insurance, or spend hours fighting. If the company withdraws a bad claim only when someone gets enough attention, everyone else still has to decide whether contesting it is worth the trouble. I’ve called rental car fees the scammiest in travel. These damage add-ons are especially difficult to comparison shop because you don’t discover them until after you’ve returned the car. Sixt Isn’t Great, But You Expect Charges To Be Correct I’ve found Sixt offers an inferior experience in the U.S. market. My Miami rental years ago involved a Mercedes they didn’t and a proposed alternative of a $30 a day upgrade for a lesser car. I canceled and went to National. The Milwaukee airport said its lease requires Sixt to follow the law and allows termination for an uncured violation after notice. But the airport said it was waiting for the state consumer protection agency to determine that a violation occurred. It’s not yet clear whether they’ve stopped charging these fees in Wisconsin. This is common practice in Europe. Hertz sent me an invoice and charged my credit card almost a year after a rental in Germany for $460.00 for “damages.” I disputed the charges as I still had my return showing that they signed off with no damage. AMEX refunded my money, so Hertz turned it over to a collection agency in PA. They called me and I told them to go to hell and sue me. The collection dude said, “No one is going to sue you for $460.00,” so I sent them a letter telling them to cease and desist contacting me about the charge and if they wanted to sue, I was willing to counter sue as I had paperwork saying the car was returned undamaged. Last I heard of it and it never turned up on my credit report. Every time I rent in Europe, I get dinged for a toll, or in Italy it was for driving in a “congested area.” You figure they steal $100 to $200 from every renter, that is a good chunk of change a year.

Sixt got me for some damage that I know I didn’t cause. I didn’t think I needed to record video of the car after I brought it back. Credit card CDW paid for 90% of it except for a lost depreciation fee of $200. Snakey.

Im not going to no collections over a damage dispute. Ruining my credit? Pay for it and sue later.

I don’t rent cars very often, but when I do, I video the entire exterior and interior at pickup and again when I return the car along with the guy/girl I hand the keys to. I had one of these BS damage incidents several years ago and I got dinged for something I didn’t do and it was a couple months after I rented. Fortunately I was still in possession of the turn in receipt so I didn’t have to pay. All that being said, they are scam artists of the 10th degree and I don’t trust any of them.. Video and photograph your rentals.

Avis is notorious for ‘cleaning fees’. 9 times out of 10 the claim is dropped. It is important to take pics before AND after.

Maybe I’ve just been lucky, but this is (one of the reasons) why I like National. They don’t seem to want to nickel and dime you over everything. The “allowed” amount of damage is pretty generous. I’ve never had them hassle me over anything. And the refill costs if you bring a car back not full of fuel aren’t totally ridiculous either.

Wisconsin law also requires rental car companies to provide you with independent damage appraisals and a right to inspect before they can just charge you for damages. I once got billed by Avis for repairs for damage that I didn’t cause weeks after my rental. I challenged it to the Avis General Counsel’s office, pointing out that they didn’t follow the law, and they dropped the charges.

It really amazes me Congress doesn’t take on Hertz and now Sixt. This is literally a 99.9% issue. You would get so much publicity and public support.

When you're traveling for work, a canceled flight is more than a hassle. It can mean missing an important meeting or paying up for a last-minute fare.

Through the end of January 2027, Capital One is giving select business cardholders a new way to manage flight disruptions. Eligible flights booked through Capital One Business Travel will automatically include free rebooking on another airline after a qualifying cancellation or delay, with Capital One covering the new ticket up to $5,000 per traveler.

When travelers book flights through Capital One Business Travel, Capital One will monitor eligible itineraries beginning 24 hours before departure. If the flight is canceled or delayed by at least three hours, the traveler will receive a notification and gain access to a self-service rebooking tool.

The benefit covers several types of disruptions, including:

Last week's ground stop, which backed flights up for days, is a good example of when this benefit could be a huge help.

And unlike traditional airline rebooking, which may be limited to flights operated by the original carrier or its partners, Capital One's tool allows eligible travelers to select a replacement flight on another airline, with the new ticket covered up to $5,000 per traveler.

The flexibility to jump to a competing airline is the standout feature. When one carrier is sold out, another airline may still have space. Re-routing through a different connecting airport can also be strategic to avoid weather issues altogether.

Replacement flights must depart on the same or following day, serve the original destination or a nearby airport and be booked in the same (or lower) fare class. Despite these terms, this will still give travelers far more flexibility than handling things independently.

Travelers can also contact a live agent for 24/7 support.

Capital One Business Travel is available to cardholders with several Capital One business cards, including the following:

Holding one of these cards does not guarantee the free add-on. To check, log in to Capital One Business Travel. If the complimentary rebooking feature is available to you, it will be automatically added to your eligible flight at checkout.

The Venture X Business is particularly relevant for frequent flyers because it earns 5 miles per dollar spent on flights booked through Capital One Business Travel. Plus, it comes with a $300 annual credit for bookings made through Capital One Business Travel.

New applicants can potentially get even more value from Capital One Business Travel through the card's current welcome offer, which includes up to 300,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 travel credit after meeting two spending thresholds:

The information for the Capital One Spark Classic for Business, Capital One Spark Miles for Business, Capital One Spark Miles Select for Business, Capital One Spark Pro and Capital One Spark Classic Miles for Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Related: Capital One Venture X Business review: High earning rates and premium perks for businesses

This is useful protection, but it comes with restrictions. The original ticket must be booked through Capital One Business Travel, and the disruption must meet the three-hour threshold within 24 hours of departure.

It's also temporary. The complimentary is available for eligible bookings made through the end of January 2027, while supplies last. Capital One hasn't published a final eligible departure date.

Still, this could be valuable for business travelers with time-sensitive trips. It can also eliminate business travel bottlenecks, such as waiting for a manager to approve a costly replacement ticket.

Related: Getting a refund for a canceled or delayed flight

Capital One's new feature will help you with rebooking options, but it won't cover the other costs of getting stranded.

For example, if you're rebooked on a flight the following day, you may need to pay for a hotel, meals or transportation. That's where eligible credit card trip delay coverage could help.

Trip delay insurance covers unexpected costs related to qualifying delays, such as accommodations, meals or transportation while waiting out your delay.

That gap can be especially important during weather or air traffic control disruptions, when airlines generally do not pay for stranded travelers' hotels or meals.

Not every eligible card includes trip delay coverage, though. The Venture X Business covers up to $500 per ticket for meals and lodging when a trip is delayed six hours or more or requires an overnight stay.* Cash-back cards like the Spark Cash don't include it. Check your card's benefits guide before you travel.

Related: Flight delayed? 4 things to do to get trip delay reimbursement from your credit card

Capital One's complimentary flight disruption rebooking could be a valuable perk for business travelers facing cancellations or lengthy delays, particularly when another airline can get them to their destination sooner.

And it costs you nothing extra when booking on Capital One Business Travel.

The promotion is available to select Capital One customers for a limited time, so check whether the benefit appears at checkout before relying on it for an upcoming trip.

*For Capital One products listed on this page, some of the benefits may be provided by Visa® or Mastercard® and may vary by product. See the respective Guide to Benefits for details, as terms and exclusions apply.

#6071. LATAM Unveils New Airbus A321XLR Business Class Suites, Coming March 2027

LATAM has just unveiled the full interiors for its upcoming Airbus A321XLRs, which will make it the first carrier in South America to offer fully flat suites with direct aisle access on a narrow body aircraft. These planes are expected to enter service in the coming months, so we won’t have to wait much longer to fly them!

LATAM has 13 Airbus A321XLRs are on order, which are expected to enter service as of March 2027. The A321XLR is the new long range, narrow body aircraft from Airbus, which stretches the capabilities of the A321 family.

The airline intends to use these planes to open up new long haul markets, though it’s not yet clear out of which LATAM hubs the planes will fly. I suspect these planes will primarily be used for service to North America, or possibly for service from secondary cities in Brazil to Europe. Officially, for now the airline just claims these planes will be used to “strengthen connectivity between South America and more distant destinations.”

Earlier this year, LATAM’s CEO did drop some hints that the plane could fly from Lima (LIM) and Brasilia (BSB) to the United States, and from Fortaleza (FOR) to Europe, though no final decisions have been announced.

We can expect LATAM to offer an all-new passenger experience (by the carrier’s standards) onboard the Airbus A321XLRs. The airline plans to configure the planes with a total of 174 seats, including:

Throughout the plane, passengers can expect the Panasonic Astrova entertainment system, with over 2,300 hours of content, including 330 movies and 1,200 TV shows. Bluetooth audio will also be available at all seats, so that passengers can connect to their own headphones. The A321XLR will also be equipped with SES Wi-Fi, with LATAM Pass members getting complimentary browsing or messaging, depending on their membership tier and ticket type.

LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product. So there will be 12 herringbone seats in a 1-1 configuration, with seats spread across six rows. This means all seats will have direct aisle access and doors. Business class seats will feature 19″ 4K OLED screens, AC power outlets, USB-C charging, and wireless charging.

It also looks like the front row seats will be pretty special, as they’ll feature quite a bit of extra space, including a closet and wardrobe. It remains to be seen how the airline will monetize that extra space, if at all (maybe they’ll just be reserved for certain types of passengers?).

LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Recaro R3 product. So there will be 162 seats in a 3-3 configuration, with six rows having extra legroom, and 21 rows having standard legroom. Economy class seats will feature 13″ 4K OLED screens, as well as USB-C outlets.

The A321XLR is impressive for its range, and it’s understandable that the economics of such a small plane for long haul flying can be challenging. As a result, we’re really seeing airlines try to maximize capacity as much as possible, and this is also leading to so many airlines having very similar premium products on planes.

LATAM will have herringbone seats on the A321XLR, just like… well, all current operators that use this primarily as a long haul aircraft, with the exception of Aer Lingus.

For those keeping track at home, the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product is what you’ll find in JetBlue’s Mint business class on select A321neo/LR aircraft, and it’s also what you’ll find in Iberia’s A321XLR business class.

While American’s A321XLR business class looks similar, it’s based on the Collins Aerospace Aurora seating platform, and that’s also what Air Canada has selected. Meanwhile United’s A321XLR business class also looks similar, but is based on the Elevate Altitude platform.

Admittedly these planes all have better business class products than we found on long haul Boeing 757s years ago (the most direct replacement), and the tech is also greatly updated. That being said, as a passenger experience geek, this sure is a boring plane… “you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, everyone gets a herringbone seat!”

While not quite A321XLRs, credit to ITA Airways’ A321neo business class and Etihad’s A321LR business class for having reverse herringbone seats.

To LATAM’s credit, I will say that the cabin finishes look gorgeous, so I hope they look as nice in real life as they do in renderings.

In early 2027, LATAM expects to start taking delivery of the Airbus A321XLR, which the airline plans to use to grow into new markets. The airline has now revealed what we can expect onboard these planes, and it includes herringbone seats with direct aisle access and doors in business class.

Ultimately the cabin looks sleek, and it’s cool to see this in South America, where no other airline is currently offering such an experience. But still, it’s hard to get too excited when so many airlines are introducing a similar product.

LATAM in general deserves credit for the extent to which it’s elevating the passenger experience in Latin America, as we’ve seen the airline introduce two new wide body business class products over the past several years.

What do you make of LATAM’s new A321XLR business class?

#6070. American Airlines Plans To Nearly Triple Its Phoenix A Gates Lounge Space—And Add 150% More Seats

American Airlines Phoenix lounges are one of the biggest holes in the airline’s effort to offer a better product. They’re been too small, crowded dated, and barely worth visiting even when you have access. Already American expects 18 million lounge visits in 2026 up 80% from 10 million in 2016 while passenger traffic is up just 12.1%. What may have worked in the past no longer does. And American is finally announcing substantial investment in all three Admirals Clubs, adding enough room that getting away from a crowded gate might actually mean getting away from a crowd. Here’s what’s changing: Location   Planned Changes A19–A21   Near term: new food service area, infrastructure for expanded food and drink offerings, and facility updates. B5–B7   New self-service food and beverage area, 20% more seats, refreshed interiors and improved support space. Both A clubs, including A7–A9   Longer term: nearly triple their combined footprint, approximately 150% more seats, and refreshed furnishings and finishes. A club seating would become about 2.5 times current level. American isn’t sharing expected completion dates, actual seat counts or square footage. And there’s no Phoenix Flagship Lounge announcement. What’s perhaps most interesting to me is they’re spending on Terminal 4 even as they committed to invest as the anchor airline for Phoenix’s planned $4.5 billion West Terminal. The airport expects a late 2033 opening (so sometime after that, natch). That’s seven years away. American can’t sell a premium experience today on the promise that its lounges will become better in the mid-2030s. But the American I’ve come to known wouldn’t invest today when they’ll also be investing later. Phoenix unveiled its preferred West Terminal concept at Tuesday’s Industry Day, which American CEO Robert Isom attended. So the timing of this announcement wasn’t a coincidence. American, though, is investing in its lounges in a real turnaround. I suggested last year that I’d believe their commitment to becoming a more premium carrier and focusing on revenue growth rather than just cost control when the capital investments started – clubs and new planes. We’re still waitin on the expected aircraft order, but American is planning to deliver a new, renovated or expanded lounge nearly every month on average over two to three years. Phoenix had been a real omission from the announced pipeline. After years of club closures and renovations I described as “modern hospital,” American developed a much warmer design. Washington National’s E concourse club, followed by Denver, Newark and Philadelphia, showed what they could do with better lighting, wood, and places that are actually comfortable to sit and work. The food has been improving as well. I covered the additional hot dishes and better charcuterie in Admirals Clubs. And Flagship lounge food is getting better. Flagship Dining now offers sit down meals and good wine for long haul business class passengers. The current lounge pipeline includes: Airport   Project Charlotte   More than 40,000 square feet above the atrium, plus a separately announced Flagship Lounge. Dallas–Fort Worth   A 37,000 square foot Terminal C club and Terminal F Provisions. Miami   A new Flagship Lounge and expanded D30 Admirals Club, nearly doubling total lounge space. Chicago O’Hare   A replacement Concourse L club exceeding 10,000 square feet. Washington National   Rebuilding the D club with 50% more seats. Austin   More than 12,000 square feet with an outdoor terrace. Permits are in hand, and I expect a 2027 opening. Nashville   About 17,400 square feet with outdoor terraces. Construction is targeted for 2027. New York JFK   A 3,700 square foot Provisions location with a dedicated barista bar. San Antonio’s new terminal plans also include its first Admirals Club. And Los Angeles Flagship Dining reopened November 5. American announced Citi branding at Admirals Club entrances. It’s part of their new card agreement that is more of a joint venture than supplier relationship. Citi gets an airport lounge presence through American’s network. The Executive card includes membership, while Globe and Strata Elite each provide four passes a year. The clubs help sell three different credit cards. Lounge pricing pushes frequent flyers toward Citi. The Executive card’s annual fee is $695 for new applicants. A full standalone Admirals Club membership is $1,200–$1,400, while even the restricted $750 Single membership costs more than the card and leaves out guests and partner lounges. American is making the card the obvious way to buy access. Better clubs help get customers to apply and give them a reason to renew. Once they’re carrying the card, American and Citi have more opportunities to get their spending. And with Globe and Strata Elite distributing passes alongside Executive memberships, American needs more seats./ Topics on this pageAdmirals ClubAirport loungeAmerican AirlinesCitibankPhoenix Sky Harbor International AirportAustinChicagoDenverMiamiNashvilleNew YorkO'HarePhiladelphiaPhoenixRobert IsomSan AntonioTerminal 4+12 more More From View from the Wing

Already American expects 18 million lounge visits in 2026 up 80% from 10 million in 2016 while passenger traffic is up just 12.1%. What may have worked in the past no longer does.

And American is finally announcing substantial investment in all three Admirals Clubs, adding enough room that getting away from a crowded gate might actually mean getting away from a crowd.

A club seating would become about 2.5 times current level. American isn’t sharing expected completion dates, actual seat counts or square footage. And there’s no Phoenix Flagship Lounge announcement.

What’s perhaps most interesting to me is they’re spending on Terminal 4 even as they committed to invest as the anchor airline for Phoenix’s planned $4.5 billion West Terminal.

The airport expects a late 2033 opening (so sometime after that, natch). That’s seven years away. American can’t sell a premium experience today on the promise that its lounges will become better in the mid-2030s. But the American I’ve come to known wouldn’t invest today when they’ll also be investing later.

Phoenix unveiled its preferred West Terminal concept at Tuesday’s Industry Day, which American CEO Robert Isom attended. So the timing of this announcement wasn’t a coincidence.

American, though, is investing in its lounges in a real turnaround. I suggested last year that I’d believe their commitment to becoming a more premium carrier and focusing on revenue growth rather than just cost control when the capital investments started – clubs and new planes. We’re still waitin on the expected aircraft order, but American is planning to deliver a new, renovated or expanded lounge nearly every month on average over two to three years. Phoenix had been a real omission from the announced pipeline.

After years of club closures and renovations I described as “modern hospital,” American developed a much warmer design. Washington National’s E concourse club, followed by Denver, Newark and Philadelphia, showed what they could do with better lighting, wood, and places that are actually comfortable to sit and work.

The food has been improving as well. I covered the additional hot dishes and better charcuterie in Admirals Clubs. And Flagship lounge food is getting better. Flagship Dining now offers sit down meals and good wine for long haul business class passengers.

San Antonio’s new terminal plans also include its first Admirals Club. And Los Angeles Flagship Dining reopened November 5.

American announced Citi branding at Admirals Club entrances. It’s part of their new card agreement that is more of a joint venture than supplier relationship. Citi gets an airport lounge presence through American’s network. The Executive card includes membership, while Globe and Strata Elite each provide four passes a year. The clubs help sell three different credit cards.

Lounge pricing pushes frequent flyers toward Citi. The Executive card’s annual fee is $695 for new applicants. A full standalone Admirals Club membership is $1,200–$1,400, while even the restricted $750 Single membership costs more than the card and leaves out guests and partner lounges.

American is making the card the obvious way to buy access. Better clubs help get customers to apply and give them a reason to renew. Once they’re carrying the card, American and Citi have more opportunities to get their spending. And with Globe and Strata Elite distributing passes alongside Executive memberships, American needs more seats./

#6069. She Lived to the Sound of God’s Music

Remembering God’s gift to New York City girls and beyond.

From left: Sr. Christine Cosgrove, O.P., the author, Sr. Martha Kunesh, O.P., and speaker Kristen Hanson, an advocate against assisted suicide, at a National Review Institute/Sheen Center event on the virtue of hope.

Could anything sound more exotic today? This opening line comes from a 16th-century prayer by the Carmelite reformer St. Teresa of Avila. She carried it in the breviary she used for daily prayer. It also captures the quiet steadiness of Sister Martha Kunesh, O.P. (the initials stand for “Order of Preachers”), who entered a Dominican convent just before the opening of the Second Vatican Council. She took the religious name Sister Teresa Avila (“the ‘of’ was silent,” it was said). She eventually returned to her birth name, but she never lost the contemplative spirit of her first patron.

#6067. Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”

Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from new software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin said “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

“This is an emergency,” he said. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin said the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

“We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin said. "Nickel and diming it together does not work."

Thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications."

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment."

Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

The 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

The committee’s majority said Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a new one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

“Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell said.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and said their committee would “thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop.”

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

At issue in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have said they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

It's here! Frontier Airlines is now offering its GoWild All You Can Fly Pass for 2027, letting travelers take to the skies at a deep discount for an entire year (and potentially longer).

For a limited time, flyers can purchase a GoWild Pass good through 2027 for just $399. Members of the airline's Discount Den can score the pass for $349.

While that's not quite as good as some offers we've seen in past years (but better than some in other years), it can add up to significant savings if you fly the airline a lot. You must be a Frontier Miles member to purchase one.

Keep in mind that passholders pay $0.01 in airfare plus applicable taxes, fees and charges at the time of booking, so the pass gets you out of the regular airfare, but you're still on the hook for taxes and fees as well as other charges for things like optional seat selection and bags. While taxes on domestic legs are low, international ones can incur $60-$110 each way, depending on the destination.

Sneak peek: Frontier's new first-class seats are finally on sale, set for March debut

Multiple passholders can book travel at the same time, but you can't mix and match passholders with non-passholders on the same reservation.

Likewise, different types of fares can be combined each way on itineraries as long as all passengers hold a valid GoWild Pass at the time of booking and the primary passenger holds a Discount Den membership if Discount Den fares are selected.

One other big caveat: GoWild passes autorenew, so if you want to cancel when your current pass expires, you'll need to contact the airline to do so. Your renewal date will be stated in your confirmation email when purchasing the pass.

The GoWild Pass is valid for flights to over 100 destinations across Frontier's route network, including both domestic gateways and international cities in Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America. The airline's route network changes frequently, though, so stay on top of it to make sure your route will be in service when it's time to book.

Travel begins after purchase (meaning as soon as today) and is available through Dec. 31, 2027, meaning potentially over a full year of flying.

There are no blackout dates, like we've seen in some past instances, but on peak dates, you can expect to pay $59-$199 extra per segment.

Here's the kicker: Standard bookings for eligible GoWild fares begin a day before departure for domestic flights and 10 days before departure for international flights. If your return flight is outside that window, then you'll have to try to make an additional booking when the window opens for that flight.

If you do want to book more in advance than that, however, you can pay an additional charge to do so, though this can vary based on the date and the route.

Also keep in mind that just because a seat is open on the flight you want does not mean it's eligible for a GoWild booking.

You can earn Frontier Miles on the purchase of the pass as well as any extras, like seat assignments, bag fees or priority boarding that you purchase.

If you hold elite status with Frontier, you are still eligible for your benefits, including free seats and bags, so that can be a great way to save on optional fees that non-elites have to pay.

All-you-can-fly airline passes are a rarity these days and come with lots of limitations. Frontier Airlines' GoWild All You Can Fly Pass is no exception.

Still, if you fly the airline a lot, have flexibility (and a bit of spontaneity) in your plans and don't need a ton of extra amenities like preferred seats or checked bags, these fares can be a good way to save a bit on flights you'd be taking anyway ... or perhaps some fun last-minute fares you wouldn't be able to take advantage of otherwise.

#6065. Standing Athwart Pumpkin Tyranny

Through October and November, this mediocre flavor and scent are in everything everywhere all the time.

A display of Trader Joe’s pumpkin and fall-themed products at a grocery store in Lafayette, Calif., September 25, 2026.

A pumpkin spice latte is on the menu at every coffee shop. Sometimes, the drink is served in a pumpkin-shaped mug. To lure in customers for brunch, quaint cafes serving pumpkin pancakes put a chalkboard sign on the sidewalk saying, “COME IN FOR GOURD VIBRATIONS!” Each bakery has pumpkin scones, pumpkin pie, pumpkin banana bread, and pumpkin coffee cake. An attempt to order an old fashioned will be met with an invitation from the demoralized bartender, “Do you want to try our pumpkin spice old fashioned?” The pen at the bank is topped with a rubber pumpkin; this way, customers know that all the money is kept safe. Little plastic pumpkins are in the windows displays at clothing shops, or beside the cashiers (who work in front of pumpkin-flavored nicotine patches). Squashes are piled high in cardboard bins by the entrance of every grocery store. I reach for what I think is my favorite chai tea blend on the shelves — but alas! It is now pumpkin chai with an orange label.

Through October and November, pumpkin is in everything everywhere all the time. Anything edible is infused, swirled, drizzled, and dusted with pumpkin. You cannot escape the flavor: pumpkin cereal, pumpkin protein powder, pumpkin bagels with pumpkin cream cheese. The Asian aisle has frozen Kung Pao-mpkin Dumplings. Dog treats are flavored like a pumpkin spice latte because everyone must participate, no exceptions. Longstanding favorites are replaced, so French fries are now pumpkin fries. That peculiar squash always sneaks its way into a dish, and so the stuffed raviolis have a little bit of pumpkin. Despite its omnipresence, the pumpkin surprises you: The waiter arrives at the table with a salad that is topped — just for this week — with toasted pumpkin seeds. (Of course, the utensils are wrapped in a flimsy brown napkin dotted with little orange pumpkins.) Even things we thought were reliably mint, like gum and the dentist’s fluoride, are pumpkin spice.

Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

#6063. Climate Change Could Squeeze a Third of Tourist Destinations by 2050

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Climate change won’t just bring more extreme weather. It will shorten the seasons and change the activities many destinations are built on. Operators should be planning now for shoulder seasons and cooler-hour itineraries, not waiting for the next heat wave.

Climate change is coming for the tourist season.

More than a third of destinations could see conditions for sightseeing, swimming and hiking worsen by 2050, according to a new report, and some of travel’s biggest beach regions could lose months of good weather.

The report, by NGO Travel Forward, risk modeling firm Risklayer, and the Dutch public-private partnership Centre of Expertise Leisure, Tourism and Hospitality (CELTH), models climate hazards and conditions for common tourist activities across 2,588 destinations in 263 countries and territories.

Called Destination Climate RiskScan, it found that 36% of destinations would be “squeezed” by 2050 under a moderate emissions scenario, facing more extreme weather and a climate less suited to common tourism activities. That  percentage soars to 62% by 2050 under a high emission scenario.

A new report modeling climate conditions across 2,588 destinations in 263 countries finds that 36% of them could be "squeezed" by 2050 under a moderate emissions scenario — facing more climate hazards alongside worse conditions for sightseeing, swimming, hiking, and camping — with that figure rising to 62% under high emissions. The Destination Climate RiskScan, produced by NGO Travel Forward, risk modeling firm Risklayer, and Dutch partnership CELTH, scores hazard exposure and activity suitability on a 0–100 index. The steepest declines land in the hottest regions: Caribbean hiking and camping could fall 53 points by 2080 under high emissions, Southeast Asian swimming 48 points, and Mediterranean hiking and camping 48 points. Southeast Asia's typical beach and swimming season could shrink from eight months in 2010 to three by 2080, and the Caribbean's from 10 to six. Northern Europe and the Nordics are projected to become more comfortable for every activity assessed except skiing, though the ski model excluded artificial snowmaking. The authors stress these are measures of climatic suitability, not forecasts of visitor demand or commercial viability. The report lands as policymakers meet at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, where tourism is a thematic focus.

The lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are currently scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen said Sunday on CNN.

​Van Hollen has also said he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A new issue is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Fox News Sunday.

Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

"We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy said in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel."

Meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

On the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

New member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

That includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is currently the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.

#6052. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

#6051. Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his new memoir, Biden said he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

In conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s new book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major issues of our time.

It’s often said that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

The sheer length of his new book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

Supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single issue in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”

Recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

“We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he says. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”

One of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

“I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

“The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling showed only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

Describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he says there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”

“I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden says. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

“I had it on good authority that several big names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

Biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

#6050. What Pro-Lifers Need to Win Elections

In election after election, pro-lifers are being outspent and outorganized.

Demonstrators participate in the annual March for Life in Washington, D.C., January 23, 2026.

It’s become something of a truism that the pro-life movement lacked a plan for how to pursue its goals after Roe v. Wade was overturned. Indeed, three more states (Nevada, Virginia, and Missouri) saw abortion-related statewide ballot measures go against pro-lifers in 2026. The recriminations have been bitter against the leaders and key advocacy groups on the pro-life side: They are political naifs; they are incompetent at messaging and strategy; they are self-important, wannabe big shots who just want proximity to power; they are too focused on federal politics; their organizations’ CEOs make too much money (hilariously false — ask me how I know) for too little results.

There is plenty of blame to go around, but I think such critiques are missing the key, practical problems the pro-life movement faces. The reality is that the pro-abortion side simply has far more money and organization than the pro-life side, and these gaps have been decisive in election after election. Without the funding for political organization and campaigns, pro-lifers simply cannot win.

#6047. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

#6046. “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.

Compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: his corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

All it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie. By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

Performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

And this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout “Subsequent Movefilm” for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment we’re introduced to Bakalova’s Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

Tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on par with the sinking of the Titanic. Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, “the happiest wife in the world,” emboldening her to join Borat’s latest trip as a stowaway.

Similarly life, and Borat’s government, have not been kind to him since “Cultural Learnings” conquered America with great success – high five! – 14 years ago.

America may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

When Kazakhstan’s current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, he’s hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form – ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all – and given a new mission to smooth glorious leader’s entry into the world’s strongman club. How? By presenting to”Vice Premier Mikhail Pence” valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, “Kazakhstan’s Minister of Culture and No.1 porno star.”

This is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the film’s release fails to ruin “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas,  plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one announced in the film’s full title: “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

In the main, the humor driving “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series “Who Is America?” – which is to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

Now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

The sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way into the psyche of the ugly American – enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit he’d pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. “They’re fun!”

Following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, “Subsequent Moviefilm” makes Tutar’s empowerment the centerpiece of the movie’s second half.  Baron Cohen’s signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Woliner’s past TV work (which includes series such as “Nathan for You”) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

Either way, the fact that “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

There’s the practical matter that the character of Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen announced that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that “the problem with success, although it’s fantastic, is that every new person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I ‘get’ with Borat again, so it’s a kind of self-defeating form, really.”

What he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today. However, he’s right about the problem of Borat’s fame. “Subsequent Moviefilm” confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

Nonetheless, Borat’s relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant — except for when he revealshis subjects’ prejudices.

But then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original “Borat” don’t involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Borat’s stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

Fewer of those sight gags exist in “Subsequent Moviefilm.” Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctor’s office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

Then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohen’s infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama “with the Wuhan flu.”

Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business don’t tell us anything we don’t already know. Instead, it’s what the context implies about America’s psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isn’t merely in the pastor’s misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutar’s stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutar’s father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?)

But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesn’t disturb the status quo.

There’s the Texas baker who uses icing to pipe the words “Jews Will Not Replace Us” on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. There’s the shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the “no means yes” dress section. There’s the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, “What color is best for racist family?” says without pause or reaction, “I wouldn’t go any darker than a six or a seven.”

This leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; she’s also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first “Borat” and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, she’s a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

Evaluating the comedy value of “Subsequent Moviefilm” relative to the first “Borat” sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has aren’t deadly, although it’s plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the film’s ending in ways that don’t feel fully baked.

The most prominent difference between the “Borat” of 2006 and the 2020 “Subsequent Moviefilm” is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trump’s election in 2016, to say nothing of how decline and fall of basic critical thought has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

At the same time, there’s simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If there’s a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called “lesser” nations.

Now it doesn’t allow the audience to be so sure of itself, implying in the final scene that we aren’t merely ugly Americans. We’re a once glorious nation being led by goons who are sliding us backward into diminishment, and dangerously so. That is nothing to laugh about.

“Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” is currently streaming on Amazon.

#6045. The AI Agent Is Travel’s Ad Blocker

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: AI agents can block impulse purchases. Grok

Travel companies have built profitable businesses around persuading customers to spend more. AI agents working for travelers may be harder to persuade.

Travel companies make money from impulse purchases. A traveler sees a better seat, a room upgrade, or another offer at checkout and decides to spend more. An AI agent booking on that traveler's behalf doesn't buy on impulse. That’s the concern MCR Hotels CEO Tyler Morse raised at our Skift Commerce Summit earlier this month, and it’s a risk to the upsells that drive a large share of many travel companies’ profits.

Wall Street is focused elsewhere. In a November 15 report, analysts at Citizens tested two AI booking agents, Instinct and Meta's Muse. They found the experience “underwhelming” but saw significant long-term risks for online travel agencies, ranking Expedia as the most exposed, followed by Booking Holdings, with Airbnb the most insulated.

The analysts focused on who would capture the booking and how much commission they could charge. Morgan Stanley's October analysis examined similar questions.
