Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

A colleague in the intelligence community once jokingly called me a “Chinese spy.” His casual remark is burned into my memory. I am a Taiwanese American who has served as a U.S. intelligence officer and worked on semiconductor policy for the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party. Even while serving this country, my loyalty could become a punchline.

The Jensen Huang scandal now tests Washington’s ability to keep that reflex out of national security policy. He resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Nov. 12, just days after reports of his relationships with businesswoman Alice Huang and a company executive. Yet his abrupt departure leaves serious questions related to Chinese espionage unresolved. Investigators must still determine whether Jensen Huang helped Beijing obtain secrets or influence.

A colleague in the intelligence community once jokingly called me a “Chinese spy.” His casual remark is burned into my memory. I am a Taiwanese American who has served as a U.S. intelligence officer and worked on semiconductor policy for the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party. Even while serving this country, my loyalty could become a punchline.

The Jensen Huang scandal now tests Washington’s ability to keep that reflex out of national security policy. He resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Nov. 12, just days after reports of his relationships with businesswoman Alice Huang and a company executive. Yet his abrupt departure leaves serious questions related to Chinese espionage unresolved. Investigators must still determine whether Jensen Huang helped Beijing obtain secrets or influence.

In the meantime, public discourse in the United States is conflating the potential for Chinese coercion with the proof of its existence, even going so far as to promote ethnic scapegoating. The growing hysteria is increasingly focused on the threat posed by anyone at all associated with China. The irony is that this will eventually, in concrete ways, make Americans less secure.

News reports described intercepted communications suggesting that Chinese intelligence received information from someone close to Jensen Huang and Nvidia. It also reported that federal officials have been investigating whether Alice Huang’s Megaspeed has been potentially diverting restricted Nvidia chips to China since 2024. If true, Washington should prosecute those involved and close relevant loopholes.

Reporting has also described, however, a troubling divide within the U.S. government. Some intelligence officials considered the spy label “over-torqued.” Attorney General Todd Blanche and Rep. Jim Himes, a ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee, also weighed in on the day that Jensen Huang resigned, saying neither the U.S. Justice Department nor the intelligence community had concluded she was a spy; while her reported proximity to Jensen Huang justifies scrutiny, it cannot by itself prove that she worked for Beijing.

Either way, nothing about this case makes all people of Asian descent suspect. Jensen Huang’s conduct deserves scrutiny; the loyalty of millions who share his ancestry does not. And yet Congress is beginning to overstep from proper oversight into broader exclusion. Rep. Riley Moore’s bill, for example, proposes denying student and exchange visas for research or study to Chinese nationals. Adopting that approach in response to Nvidia solely because of someone’s nationality fails to address actual security vulnerabilities.

Washington could and should proactively mitigate threats; foreign intelligence ties, risky financial exposure, and transferring unauthorized information are legitimate reasons to restrict sensitive access. But the idea that every Chinese citizen could be a spy dangerously conflates vulnerability with culpability.

It’s true that China’s national intelligence law compels citizens and organizations to assist intelligence work. Beijing can pressure its citizens, but that does not automatically make them a Chinese agent. In 2018, William Evanina, then the United States’ top counterintelligence official, noted that 99.9 percent of Chinese students in the United States were “here legitimately and doing great research.” Most may never be approached by China’s Ministry of State Security, and others might simply refuse or report such encounters. Effective counterintelligence cannot consider these all as equivalent.

The current public discourse is also actively blurring the clear distinction between Chinese ancestry and Chinese citizenship. The Asian American Journalists Association called out headlines that turned Jensen Huang’s surname into an espionage pun. On X, a viral collage highlighted prominent executives married to women of Chinese descent with the caption, “I have one question… actually, a LOT of questions.” Another post invoked “Chinese honeypot espionage” in reference to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s former roommate, Chinese American AI executive Alexandr Wang.

In a 2019 bill that Trump signed into law, Congress warned that profiling plays right into Beijing’s narrative that the global Chinese diaspora owes it loyalty. Washington should not validate that claim.

Blanket suspicion makes legitimate threats harder to identify. MITRE’s insider threat researchers warned that indiscriminate threat indicators overwhelm security with false positives. Nationality alone cannot distinguish a Chinese agent from a dissident resisting Beijing. Pursuing imagined spies can leave real ones undetected.

Profiling also silences those best positioned to expose espionage. The FBI warns of various ways that foreign governments may coerce their citizens in the United States to serve their interests. A threatened scientist could help investigators neutralize foreign intelligence activity early. If speaking up invites suspicion, though, they will likely remain silent.

Trust is critical to improving security. In April 2025, Taiwan’s Defense Ministry found that voluntary reporting prompted 87.5 percent of national security investigations. Beijing’s preferred targets are often best positioned to expose its operations. Washington should make reporting foreign coercion safer through confidential channels backed by legal and security assistance.

Unwarranted suspicion also threatens the United States’ AI talent lead over China. A recent study by Carnegie Endowment found that 57 percent of authors accepted to NeurIPS 2025, one of the most elite AI conferences, had earned undergraduate degrees in China. Only 13 percent had gone to college in the United States. Furthermore, China now hosts 41 percent of the world’s top AI researchers. The United States is down to 34 percent, flipping its 2022 advantage. Washington cannot afford to alienate these scientists.

A 2023 study found that 89 percent of Chinese researchers at U.S. universities desired American scientific leadership, yet nearly two-thirds had considered leaving the country. The United States risks losing the scientists who want to help it lead. Treating them as presumptive threats could hand the U.S. talent advantage to Beijing.

The United States has made this mistake before. In 1950, Washington stripped Qian Xuesen, one of the country’s leading rocket scientists, of his security clearance. The FBI suspected that he was tied to communists but failed to uncover evidence of espionage. Due to his rocketry expertise, however, security officials struggled between deporting or detaining him. When Qian finally left in 1955, he spearheaded China’s formidable missile and space programs. Washington considered him too dangerous to trust and too valuable to let go. It lost him anyway.

Before pursuing charges or major research sanctions, security officers should mandate independent technical review and offer researchers due process, presuming innocence until proven guilty. In 2015, prosecutors charged Temple University physicist Xiaoxing Xi with sending proprietary technology to China. They eventually dropped the case after finding that he actually shared nonsensitive devices, but his reputation was already destroyed.

Congress already requires that federal research agencies avoid discriminating based on race, ethnicity, or national origin. Yet a January 2026 Government Accountability Office report found that five major agencies had still not evaluated their anti-discrimination safeguards. Washington should conduct those assessments to ensure all researchers are equally scrutinized based on their conduct.

Jensen Huang’s successes and failures do not make Asian Americans more or less American. Washington can and should investigate espionage without ethnically profiling Asian Americans. Otherwise, the United States risks overlooking real spies, silencing whistleblowers, and driving away world-class talent. The country’s great strength is its ability to distinguish friend from foe. It cannot afford to confuse the two.

#5915. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”

Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

For his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

“I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”

Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

“This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”

He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

“I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”

Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”

The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#5912. A Recipe for Disaster in Taiwan

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

REBECCA LISSNER is Senior Fellow for U.S. Foreign Policy and Director of the Future of American Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. She served as Deputy Assistant to the President and Principal Deputy National Security Adviser to the Vice President during the Biden administration.

MIRA RAPP-HOOPER is a Visiting Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. She was Special Assistant to the President and Senior Director for East Asia and Oceania and Director for Indo-Pacific Strategy at the U.S. National Security Council during the Biden administration.

Just a few years ago, U.S. President Joe Biden caused a stir when he confirmed publicly that his administration would defend Taiwan if the island were attacked by China—a divergence from the traditional U.S. policy of strategic ambiguity, in which Washington does not commit to taking any particular action. In May, U.S. President Donald Trump made waves for taking a different position. In a television interview, he described Taiwan as “a very good negotiating chip” in dealings with Beijing and mused that the island was close to China but far from the United States, implying that U.S. interests in Taiwan were negligible. In doing so, Trump seemed to confirm something many Asia watchers had feared: that this U.S. president would be willing to loosen the United States’ commitment to Taiwan to bolster his relationship with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

A few days later, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that there had been no change in U.S. policy toward Taiwan. But Trump’s words were alarming nonetheless—in part because they reflect a shift in Washington that goes beyond the Oval Office. Since 2025, politicians from both parties have been shying away from affirming the United States’ long-standing support for Taiwan. Meanwhile, China is developing new strategies to coerce Taiwan without going to war, and Beijing will be increasingly tempted to use them if it judges that the U.S. commitment to Taiwan is waning among both politicians and the public.

Yet that would be a grave miscalculation on China’s part. In fact, the United States’ interests in Taiwan are growing, not diminishing. Whatever the nature of Washington’s rhetoric right now, the United States would have to respond to any action by Beijing that threatened those interests, and both countries would then face a great-power crisis. To defuse this dangerous situation, American leaders must update the United States’ Taiwan strategy to reflect a new reality—and they should begin immediately.

Taiwan’s unique international status has long made U.S. policy complex. The Republic of China, now known as Taiwan, was a World War II ally of the United States. When the People’s Republic of China was founded on the mainland, in 1949, the Republic of China’s president, Chiang Kai-shek, decamped to Taiwan, and the United States maintained formal diplomatic ties with Chiang’s government, not the People’s Republic of China. In 1954, as the Cold War crested in the Pacific, the United States concluded a formal mutual defense treaty with Taiwan, in part to forestall increasingly aggressive artillery barrages from the mainland. Nearly 20 years later, however, when U.S. President Richard Nixon and his national security adviser, Henry Kissinger, began to engineer a diplomatic opening to the government in Beijing, they knew it would cost Taiwan.

In part because they understood that building diplomatic ties with Beijing would be painful for Taiwan and cause controversy in Congress, where Taipei had many boosters, Nixon and Kissinger slow-walked the process. So did Nixon’s successor, President Gerald Ford. It finally fell to President Jimmy Carter to make the change. On January 1, 1979, the United States ended its alliance with Taiwan and recognized the mainland government as “the sole legal Government of China.” Congress was irate. Lawmakers from both parties quickly drafted the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act, which remains in force. The law requires Washington to provide Taipei with defensive arms, creating the trappings of an alliance with Taiwan despite the relationship’s unofficial status. In 1982, the Reagan administration made an additional set of commitments to Taiwan, known as the Six Assurances. These include an affirmation that Washington does not endorse Beijing’s sovereignty claims over Taiwan and a promise that the United States would not use arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip.

In the 50 years since, U.S. Taiwan policy has been remarkably successful. Through its partnership and arms sales, the United States has helped underwrite peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait, and Taiwan has thrived as a democracy and an economy, even as Washington has maintained a relationship with Beijing. But U.S. commitments to Taiwan have lately come under increasing strain. China has proceeded with a massive military buildup designed to give Beijing the option to take Taiwan by force; used coercive economic tactics, launched cyberattacks, and interfered in elections to put pressure on Taipei; and run frequent army and coast guard exercises to demonstrate its ability to strangle the island. All of this has stoked concerns across the Pacific that the United States’ long-standing partnership might not be enough to keep the peace in the Taiwan Strait.

The fear that China could attempt to retake Taiwan by force, possibly during Xi’s tenure, has grown in recent years. Analysts have frequently cited 2027 as the beginning of the window of maximum danger, based on a 2021 statement made by Philip Davidson, the former commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, about when the People’s Liberation Army might be prepared for an invasion. But this timeline was never hard and fast, and Xi’s recent purge of more than 100 officers has likely delayed the military’s readiness. U.S. intelligence assessments do not anticipate an invasion of Taiwan next year, and most scholars believe the Chinese government would consider such a move as a last resort only if unification could not be accomplished by other means.

The primary danger now is that Xi will escalate a pressure campaign designed to coerce Taiwan into negotiating a change in its status. Since 2025, China’s leaders have used their diplomatic channels to the Trump administration, including Xi’s direct line to Trump, to insist on American concessions on Taiwan in exchange for progress in trade talks. In May, China secured a pause on a planned $14 billion U.S. arms sale and other defense funding for Taiwan. Beijing may hope that additional incremental moves will further weaken Taiwanese confidence in the United States and that such actions will be difficult for Trump or a future U.S. president to reverse.

China is also clearly planning for more dramatic forms of coercion. It has a few options: since 2022, China’s military has practiced blockades of Taiwan, and its coast guard has simulated a quarantine of the island’s major ports. Beijing could also use customs enforcement or other administrative measures to attempt to assert its jurisdiction over Taiwan while minimizing the likelihood that the United States would intervene to stop it. If Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, who favors Taiwanese independence but has not pursued it in office, is reelected in 2028 and Chinese leaders believe that the path to a peaceful unification is closing, Xi may consider using these tools against the island in late 2028 or early 2029, before a new U.S. administration takes office. Given Trump’s alienation of U.S. allies in Asia and Europe and Washington’s limited means to respond to a maritime quarantine, Beijing might hope to get away with such a large-scale coercion campaign without inviting serious pushback.

Taiwan’s growing strategic importance makes Beijing’s development of new coercive options more concerning. Washington is no longer maintaining a partnership with Taipei because of a historical commitment or, as Beijing would have the world believe, to needle China. The artificial intelligence boom has put Taiwan at the center of the global economy. Taiwan is a critical supplier for the U.S. tech industry, and the United States recognizes that it cannot be a leader in AI without Taiwan.

The scale of the United States’ economic dependence on Taiwan is revealing. Taiwan is the country’s fifth-largest trading partner; a Chinese blockade of the island would imperil more than $250 billion in trade and could shave more than three percent off U.S. GDP in a year, according to a Bloomberg report. As much as 97 percent of the global supply of the high-end logic chips used in smartphones and other advanced electronics are produced or packaged in Taiwan. Losing access to Taiwanese chips could reduce advanced electronics production globally by 60 percent, with factories forced to rely on their chip inventories. The United States’ auto and medical device industries could deplete their inventories in a matter of weeks. The U.S. firms Amazon, Apple, and Nvidia are among the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company’s ten largest customers, which together represent more than $14 trillion in market capitalization. With AI growth buoying the U.S. stock market and the broader economy, a crisis in Taiwan would trigger a crash—potentially one similar in scale to the stock market crash at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The economic effects of a Chinese effort to squeeze Taiwan would not be limited to the United States. The research firm Rhodium Group has conservatively estimated that a yearlong blockade of the island could cost the global economy between $2 trillion and $3 trillion. A full-scale war would be far worse; Bloomberg has estimated that it would cause $10 trillion in economic losses and a global recession. It is therefore increasingly likely that the United States would be forced to act if Taiwan’s supply chains were put in jeopardy. The cost of standing aside would simply be too high.

Yet just when the United States needs to be doing all it can to prevent a crisis, Washington’s support for Taiwan appears to be wobbling. Trump’s musings about Taiwan’s geographical distance from the United States and his use of arms sales as a bargaining chip are the headline examples, but they are not the only indicators of a shaky U.S. commitment. Policy analysts have argued that the United States should change its position to definitively oppose Taiwanese independence or even withdraw U.S. forces from the military bases in Japan and the Philippines that are closest to Taiwan.

Public opinion in the United States is shifting, too. Americans’ feelings toward China have warmed considerably over the past two years, according to a July 2026 Chicago Council on Global Affairs survey. A majority, 57 percent, support friendly cooperation and engagement with China, whereas 40 percent support an active effort to limit the growth of China’s power. The share of Americans who see China’s territorial ambitions as “a critical threat” has decreased by more than ten percentage points since 2022, and those who favor the use of U.S. troops if China invaded Taiwan has fallen from 52 percent to just 38 percent.

In part, the declining support for defending Taiwan reflects Americans’ growing wariness of instability and conflict. A sense that the world was descending into chaos helped fuel Trump’s 2024 campaign; as president, Trump has heightened that sense by taking assertive military action in places such as Iran and Venezuela. Americans are now suffering the economic consequences of nine months of war in the Middle East, further deepening antiwar sentiment, as the midterm election results vividly demonstrate. Candidates for office used to clamor to sound tough on China, but many now blanch at the idea of suggesting that the U.S. military should defend Taiwan against a Chinese invasion, calculating that this is not the time to be seen as a hawk.

Of course, public attitudes can change quickly during a crisis. If China actually committed aggression against Taiwan, Americans could become more supportive of a strong U.S. response. And if the early stages of a conflict saw American casualties or a Chinese attack on U.S. critical infrastructure, the U.S. public could very well rally around the flag and demand a muscular intervention.

For now, however, China may believe that the United States’ will and ability to fight are both diminishing. The war with Iran has substantially reduced U.S. military readiness for a Taiwan contingency. The United States has used up much of its missile defense stock, including roughly two-thirds of its Patriot interceptor inventory, which was already depleted by U.S. aid to Ukraine, and as much as 80 percent of THAAD interceptors against Iranian drones and missiles. Even before the Iran war, analysts had warned that the U.S. military could run out of long-range, precision-guided munitions in a fight over Taiwan; now, the munitions shortfalls have become perilously acute. The war has also drawn military assets away from the Indo-Pacific. In August, Washington moved its last aircraft carrier in Asia, the USS George Washington, out of the region. It has also relocated missile defense systems to the Middle East, including Patriot and THAAD systems that had been deployed in South Korea.

The result is an increased risk of dangerous miscalculation. Should Chinese leaders assess that the United States’ commitment to Taiwan is wavering in both political parties and that the country is ill prepared for a fight, they might conclude that they have an opportunity to pressure Taiwan without inviting an American response. Yet because the United States has a greater interest in Taiwan today than at any point in history, Beijing’s bet could turn out to be wrong. China could announce a maritime quarantine of Taiwan or another coercive measure only to have the United States intervene, potentially prompting a great-power standoff.

Avoiding such a showdown will require American leaders to recommit to deterrence. First, Washington needs to update the way it communicates its positions. In their public remarks, policymakers should clearly state that the U.S. economy’s dependence on Taiwanese exports makes peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait a vital interest of the United States. American political leaders should emphasize to Beijing that the United States has an obligation to prevent a crisis that would tank the U.S. stock market, cut critical supply chains, and fell many American industries.

Clarifying U.S. interests would not impugn 50 years of careful diplomacy with China, nor would it require any change to U.S. policy as established by the Taiwan Relations Act, the Six Assurances, or the series of joint U.S.-Chinese statements, made between 1972 and 1982, known as the Three Communiqués. The updated statements, rather, would convey to Chinese leaders that certain changes to the cross-strait status quo would be unacceptable to the United States, even if Taiwan were to acquiesce to those changes under pressure. Washington would support a peaceful unification, for example, only if the process guaranteed the security of critical supply chains.

Once the United States makes its interests clear, it will also have to back up its statements with a new playbook to deter Chinese actions that fall below the military threshold. Beijing may already be in the early stages of imposing a quarantine on the island. Washington should not tolerate additional measures that interfere with commerce and maritime traffic in and out of Taiwan. To deter China from taking such steps, the next U.S. Congress should use legislation to clarify its wholesale, bipartisan opposition to Chinese blockades, quarantines, and other restrictions. Even if the White House continued to take a softer position, this would send a message to Beijing that other political actors might force the president’s hand. Congress should also press the administration to prepare punitive diplomatic and financial measures for use in the event of an escalating Chinese quarantine of Taiwan. By planning these reprisals well ahead of any coercive action, Washington would signal that a maritime pressure campaign would entail clear costs for Beijing and carry dangerous escalation risks.

The United States should strengthen military deterrence, too. The next Congress must pressure the Trump administration to release the stalled $14 billion package of arms sales to Taiwan, as well as other security assistance the administration is slow-rolling. Congress has a legal obligation to do so under the Taiwan Relations Act. Pausing security aid violates U.S. policy, and allowing the Trump team to make this concession in its likely quixotic pursuit of rapprochement with Xi only weakens Washington’s hand.

Washington does not have to—and shouldn’t—take these steps alone. U.S. allies such as Germany, Japan, and South Korea would suffer nearly as much as the United States if China were to take control of Taiwan’s semiconductor industry. These countries have an interest in working quietly together to deter and develop joint responses to Chinese coercion while also collaborating to diversify their chip supply chains and make them more resilient. In the United States, this work does not have to wait for a new presidential administration. Congress can send delegations and use other diplomatic opportunities to start developing plans with parliamentary counterparts abroad.

As the 2028 U.S. presidential election approaches, moreover, candidates from both parties should speak clearly about the country’s strong economic interests in Taiwan and about their commitment to deterrence. This does not require embracing bellicose positions, but presidential candidates do need to state firmly that any move by Beijing to choke off vital supply chains would harm U.S. interests and demand an American response. Consistent messaging would also signal to China’s leaders that they should not expect a future administration to be bound by Trump’s policy concessions—and signal to allies that come 2029, the United States will again be a reliable partner in standing up to China’s economic aggression.

The United States needs to update its Taiwan policy, but ceding ground as Trump has done only makes the cross-strait balance less stable. Unlike other Cold War–era policies, the importance of preventing Chinese aggression against Taiwan has become more—not less—vital with the passage of time. U.S. interests in Taiwan are plainer and easier to explain than they have ever been. Only by stating those interests clearly and backing up the words with actions can the United States continue to avert a crisis or conflict that would be devastating for all.

#5911. The National Security Case for Permitting Reform

Analysis: The National Security Case for Permitting Reform

Power prices in the United States remain among the most affordable in the world, but any rate payer can tell you that electricity costs have been spiking across the country in recent years, due in large part to growing demand from data centers. That’s a problem not just for overstretched households but national security: for an advanced economy to be competitive globally depends on access to reliable, affordable electricity.

The United States has an array of projects ready to add electricity capacity to the grid and enable the country to distribute and store it better—but that doesn’t help when they’re stuck in a vast backlog. At the end of 2025, there were about 8,200 projects in the so-called interconnection queue—the backlog of projects waiting to be connected to the grid—representing some 1,312 gigawatts (GW) of generation capacity and 749 GW of storage capacity.

Power prices in the United States remain among the most affordable in the world, but any rate payer can tell you that electricity costs have been spiking across the country in recent years, due in large part to growing demand from data centers. That’s a problem not just for overstretched households but national security: for an advanced economy to be competitive globally depends on access to reliable, affordable electricity.

The United States has an array of projects ready to add electricity capacity to the grid and enable the country to distribute and store it better—but that doesn’t help when they’re stuck in a vast backlog. At the end of 2025, there were about 8,200 projects in the so-called interconnection queue—the backlog of projects waiting to be connected to the grid—representing some 1,312 gigawatts (GW) of generation capacity and 749 GW of storage capacity.

That’s about double the generation capacity of the entire U.S. grid. If even a fraction of this can be added, it would push down energy prices for companies and consumers alike.

This backlog, which is largely a function of limited high-capacity transmission lines and delays in federal permitting, isn’t simply an economic problem—it’s a national security risk for the United States, which is falling dangerously behind China in its rate of electrification. According to Grid Strategies, between 2021 and 2025 China built on average about 14,800 miles of high-capacity transmission per year while the United States built only 400 miles a year. The United States cannot expect to compete successfully with China in advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence, or defense production without expanding its ability to generate, transmit, and reliably deliver electricity.

Critiques of the U.S. permitting process have reached a crescendo in recent years, memorialized in books such as Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson’s Abundance and Dan Wang’s Breakneck: China’s Quest to Engineer the Future, which contrasts America’s legal culture with China’s engineer-led society. This indictment of the U.S. inability to build has adherents on the left and right, making it the rare policy area where there is the prospect of bipartisan cooperation. There’s even a “Build America” caucus in the House of Representatives focused on enhancing and expanding U.S. infrastructure.

But until recently, it looked as if permitting reform would remain a legislative pipe dream. The Trump administration’s animosity to renewable energy made it unlikely that Democrats would trust President Donald Trump to apply enhanced permitting powers evenhandedly. However, on Sept. 30, Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse alongside Republican Sens. Mike Lee and Shelley Moore Capito introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA. The since revised 494-page bill, which is slated for amendment and a vote on final passage in the Senate this week, would revolutionize how energy infrastructure gets built and paid for in the United States, including AI data centers.

The bill aims to accelerate approvals for high-voltage transmission lines and the permitting of individual projects in several ways. First, it would speed up interstate transmission by putting into statute previous guidance from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), which requires grid operators to standardize regional and joint interregional transmission planning processes.

Under BAAJA, if state or local grid operators failed to act on developers’ applications within a year, FERC would have the ability to approve important interstate power lines. Proponents of clean energy see these provisions as critical to increasing the share of renewables in the national energy mix. Solar and wind energy often need to be transmitted from where they are generated—open, rural land, or offshore—to where the demand is: cities and technology and manufacturing hubs.

The bill also sets limits on which projects require review under the National Environmental Policy Act and would speed up the process for both agency review and citizen lawsuits, which Heinrich described as a “shot clock.” This is the part of the bill that worries environmentalists the most, as it would reduce citizens’ ability to employ the courts to delay, and exercise oversight of, energy projects.

Responding to concerns that data centers are driving up consumers’ utility rates, the bill would require data centers to pay the full cost of the energy they are drawing from the existing grid, as well as the expense of expanding grid capacity for their further build-out. Because their primary objective has been the speed with which they can gain assured access to power, data centers have been increasingly installing noisy, polluting, and expensive off-grid natural gas generators to run their operations.

Doing away with these climate-damaging “behind the meter” approaches by requiring data centers to draw power from the grid itself is one area where we’d like to see this bill improved—or fixed by subsequent legislation. But advocates believe the additional energy supply that BAAJA would unlock would increasingly bring data centers into the grid without the need for further legislative intervention.

Finally, the bill’s language on permitting certainty would limit the federal government’s ability to cancel projects from sources of electricity it opposes. If compared with the previous 10 years developers can show a pattern of disparate treatment of their class of projects, whether renewables or fossil fuels, they can sue and recover costs.

Unfortunately, the bill still includes a provision that would empower the current administration, or future governments, to block or rescind permits for specific projects upon asserting that they would be harmful for U.S. national security. This sort of waiver language is common to much of the legislation that Congress passes. Under normal circumstances, this is a reasonable ask, but the current administration has abused these mechanisms to target renewable energy projects, especially wind generation, without explanation.

At present, the Defense Department runs a Siting Clearinghouse that reviews proposed energy projects to ensure they don’t interfere with military readiness, training, flight paths, radar, or testing. Over the past two years, the Trump administration has stalled its review of hundreds of wind projects, including at least 35 that had already undergone the review process and were just waiting on a final signature from department officials. When courts found these delays to be without justification, the administration offered developers some $4 billion to cancel their projects anyway. Clean energy backers argue that this de facto moratorium on processing reviews for a particular class of projects is without precedent.

If the Trump administration intends to use national security arguments to delay or obstruct renewables projects even if BAAJA passes, as his recent remarks on the topic would suggest, the expectation that renewables will fare better under a new permitting regime becomes less convincing.

Thankfully, there is a potential fix for this situation hiding in another important piece of legislation that Congress will take up in the lame-duck session: the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). Both the House and the Senate versions of the bill include language that would impose a 180-day shot clock for national security reviews to be completed, which would provide the private sector clearer planning and cost timelines. The Senate’s bill would also require the Defense Department to articulate and defend its rationale for denying any project’s permit on national security grounds.

If enacted, this NDAA provision could allay the fears of some Democrats—including former President Joe Biden’s climate czar John Podesta—that the Trump administration will weaponize BAAJA to favor fossil fuels rather than facilitating a fair contest between oil and gas and competing energy solutions.

Ultimately, the U.S. energy system is critical infrastructure. Its scale and reliability affect military installations, communications networks, transportation, financial services, industrial facilities—essentially every important component of modern society. BAAJA isn’t a perfect bill, but it should provide a path for increasing energy availability, reducing costs, and accelerating the clean energy transition, especially if the NDAA enacts safeguards on the abuse of national security exceptions. America’s strategic position may be teetering under the Trump administration, but in this age of electrification, BAAJA would enable the country to start building again—and that will increase U.S. prosperity and security alike.

Josh Busby is a professor of public affairs at the University of Texas at Austin and former senior climate advisor at the U.S. Defense Department. He is the author of States and Nature: The Effects of Climate Change on Security, which was the winner of 2026 Grawemeyer Award for Ideas Advancing World Order.

Greg Pollock is an adjunct professor at Georgetown University, where he teaches graduate students about national security risks. He previously served in a series of leadership positions in the Office of the U.S. Secretary of Defense, most recently as the acting deputy assistant secretary of defense for the Arctic and global resilience policy.

#5909. Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”

“And fortunately, I think that will fail.”

Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

“No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”

“Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”

Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

“They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”

“We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

“I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”

Several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”

Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

“Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”

“The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

“I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

“They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

“We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”

“That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”

Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”

Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

“I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”

#5908. Trump-Xi showdown revives 25-year-old Clinton China 'mistake' as Senate vet demands reversal

President Donald Trump warned Iran on Monday that it would face unprecedented retaliation if it were to carry out an attack on Washington, D.C.

Former Trump Ambassador Sam Brownback is urging Washington to reverse a decades-old trade decision and strip China of its permanent normal trade relations status, arguing the United States must rethink its economic relationship with Beijing as President Donald Trump prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

"I think it's time we back up and correct the mistake we made 25 years ago in granting normal trade relations with China, a country that seeks our demise and doesn't grant human rights, and remove that," Brownback told Fox News Digital in an interview.

Trump is traveling to China this week for his third meeting of the year with Xi, with the two leaders scheduled to hold talks Thursday in Shenzhen before joining Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral meeting, amid ongoing trade tensions and concerns over American dependence on Chinese supplies.

TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS

"I think, tactically, President Trump is playing through this right," Brownback said. "But we're in a tough spot right now."

Brownback, who served as ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom during Trump's first administration, pointed to Washington's decision more than two decades ago to establish permanent normal trade relations with China.

President Bill Clinton signed legislation authorizing permanent normal trade relations with China in 2000, and President George W. Bush formally granted the trade status in December 2001, following China's accession to the World Trade Organization.

Revoking China's permanent normal trade relations status would generally subject Chinese imports to higher tariffs, rather than automatically ending trade between the two countries.

Brownback said that reducing those dependencies and restructuring trade relations would require years rather than an immediate break with Beijing.

TRUMP SHOULD PRESS XI ON CHINA’S PERSECUTION OF BELIEVERS AT HOME AND ABROAD

Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump visit the Temple of Heaven on May 14, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Brendan Smialowski - Pool/Getty Images)

Brownback argued that the United States should now consider reversing that decision through an orderly process that would pressure Beijing to respect human rights and religious freedom.

He suggested reaching a "Helsinki Accords 2.0" deal, modeled on a landmark 1975 Cold War agreement that incorporated human rights into broader discussions between the United States, its European allies and the Soviet Union.

The agreement, Brownback said, would allow Washington to negotiate with Beijing over trade and religious freedom while warning that continued abuses could jeopardize normal trade relations.

"Either you grant human rights and religious freedom to your own people, or we're pulling back normal trade relations," Brownback said.

China's first lady Peng Liyuan, China's President Xi Jinping, President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump pose on the North Portico steps of the White House ahead of a state dinner in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 24, 2026. President Xi is on a state visit to the United States from Sept. 23 to 25. (SAUL LOEB/AFP via Getty Images)

Brownback also urged Trump to raise religious persecution directly with Xi, arguing that Beijing's treatment of Christians and other religious groups should become a central part of future negotiations.

THE CCP’S NEW ‘UNITY’ LAW TURNS CHINA’S REPRESSION INTO A GLOBAL THREAT

The U.S. Department of Labor estimated in 2022 that 100,000 Uyghurs and other ethnic minority former detainees in China may have been working under forced-labor conditions following detention in re-education camps.

"We can't trade with you if you're going to continue to operate the way you are, particularly towards people of faith, towards Christians," Brownback said.

Brownback said stabilizing the relationship would itself represent a meaningful achievement while the United States works to reduce its dependence on Chinese supplies.

"I think a successful trip is a continuation of the current situation right now, just stabilizing the relationship, not having it deteriorate further until we get in a better position on dealing with things like rare earth minerals and pharmaceutical supplies," Brownback said.

AMERICA DEPENDS TOO MUCH ON CHINA FOR ESSENTIAL MINERALS. WE NEED TO DIG OUR FUTURE

Sam Brownback urges reversing normal trade relations with China, citing human rights abuses and a long-term threat, as President Trump meets Xi Jinping. (Sarah Silbiger/Getty Images)

He also argued that religious freedom represents a strategic vulnerability for China's communist leadership, which he said views independent religious institutions as a threat to its authority.

"They now have a bigger navy than we do, but they fear religious freedom more than they do our aircraft carriers or our missiles," Brownback said.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.
